SECTION 3 - DIVISION OF DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITY 
 
3.1 
Tower Supervisor (ET Position) 
 
3.1.1 Tower Supervisor shall be responsible for: 
a) the efficiency of the control tower in accordance with relevant provisions 
b) directing the work of other ATC personnel under his charge 
c) supervising the training of Tower personnel 
d) coordinating with units providing maintenance, crash and rescue services when 
the need arises 
e) Informing Controllers of new Instruction/Circulars and any changes in 
procedure. 
f) Record any fault/irregularity/changes/status of facilities, equipment, 
g) Provide assistance at any workstation position when required by supervising, 
in particular during distress/emergency and/or security connected situation, the 
controller actions. 
h) Ensure all working position are manned 
i) Verify and provide accurate information in Daily Briefing Format 
 
 
3.2 
Subang ADC (EU Position) 
 
3.2.1 Subang ADC shall be responsible for providing a safe, orderly and expeditiously 
flow of air traffic on and in the vicinity of WMSA with the objective of preventing 
collisions between: 
a) aircraft flying in the aerodrome traffic circuit and 
b) aircraft operating on the active Runway and the entry / exit points 
 
3.2.2 He shall also be responsible for:

flow of air traffic on and in the vicinity of WMSA with the objective of preventing 
collisions between: 
a) aircraft flying in the aerodrome traffic circuit and 
b) aircraft operating on the active Runway and the entry / exit points 
 
3.2.2 He shall also be responsible for: 
a) rendering all possible assistance to aircraft in emergency or distress; and 
b) providing aircraft with meteorological and other information required for the safe 
and efficient conduct of flight. 
c) inform and/or coordinate with other position and/or unit in case of any 
situation/irregularity if necessary. 
d) training of controller on that position 
 
3.3 
Subang SMC (EV Position) 
 
3.3.1 Subang SMC shall be responsible for providing a safe, orderly and expeditiously 
flow of air traffic with the objective of preventing collisions on manoeuvring area, 
except the active Runway and the entry / exit points between: 
a) aircraft and aircraft. 
b) aircraft and vehicles. 
c) aircraft and obstructions on that area. 
 
3.3.2 He shall also be responsible for: 
a) operation of aerodrome ground lighting 
b) inform and/or coordinate with other position and/or unit in case of any 
situation/irregularity if necessary. 
c) training of controller on that position.

3.4 
Subang SMC Assistant (EW Position) 
 
3.4.1 Subang SMC Assistant shall be responsible to assist Subang SMC Assistant or 
EV position, for providing a safe, orderly and expeditiously flow of air traffic by 
coordinating and issuing of IFR and VFR ATC Clearance. 
 
3.4.2 Pilot Action to obtain ATC and Start-up/Pushback Clearance. 
a) Pilot shall obtain ATC clearance from Subang Delivery frequency before 
switching to Surface Movement Control Frequency. 
b) After receiving ATC clearance, obtain start-up and/or pushback from Surface 
Movement Control frequency. 
 
3.4.3 When necessary, Subang SMC shall merge with Subang Delivery using 
Frequency Coupling function in VCSS whenever possible. 
 
3.4.4 He shall also be responsible for training of controller on that position.

SECTION 7 - INFRINGEMENT REPORTING FOR GROUND OPERATIONS AT 
SUBANG AIRPORT 
 
7.1 
Introduction 
7.1.1 The procedure has been designed as part of safety measure to address safety 
issues such as infringements, breaches of rules and non-standard practices by 
ground operations in Subang airport. 
 
7.1.2 The objective of procedure is to improve the level of flight safety not only from the 
lesson learned from reported incidents and any subsequent follow-up action but 
also to alert Subang Aviation community of such unsafe activities. 
 
7.1.3 The objective of this requirement to report infringements is not to determine or 
apportion any blame or liability in connection with any unsafe aviation occurrences 
at Subang airport. 
 
7.1.4 The UOI is being issued to address immediately any safety issues involving 
Subang Airport Ground Operations. Other incidents involving aircraft shall be 
reported in accordance with the mandatory Occurrence Reporting Scheme 
procedures promulgated by Flight Operation Division of CAAM and the reporting 
requirements laid out in Manual of Air Traffic Services Malaysia. 
 
7.2 
Reportable Occurrence 
7.2.1 A reportable incident involving ground operations means any incident relating to 
an aircraft operation, which if not corrected, would endanger the aircraft and/or its

requirements laid out in Manual of Air Traffic Services Malaysia. 
 
7.2 
Reportable Occurrence 
7.2.1 A reportable incident involving ground operations means any incident relating to 
an aircraft operation, which if not corrected, would endanger the aircraft and/or its 
occupants and any other aircraft or person, such as towing activities that don’t 
follow procedures or breach of ATC instructions. 
 
7.2.2 A report should also be submitted on any occurrences which did not actually 
endanger the aircraft, but which if allowed to continue uncorrected or which, if 
repeated in different circumstances, could create a hazard, for example, a 
defective condition, unsatisfactory behavior or faulty procedures. 
 
7.2.3 The occurrence of other incidents that do not fall under this category shall be 
reported in accordance with other existing procedures. 
 
7.3 
Submission of Report 
7.3.1 ATCO shall immediately inform Malaysian Airports through VHF Radio, informing 
them of the incident that has occurred and subsequently record it in the log book. 
 
7.3.2 If necessary or required, Malaysian Airports Operation shall proceed immediately 
to the aircraft and escort that aircraft to an appropriate or desired location. 
 
7.3.3 The Tower Supervisor shall fill-up form “CAAM WMSA FORM IR.1” regarding the 
incident as soon as is practicable and fax it to Subang CAAM Manager and 
Malaysia Airports 
 
7.4

SECTION 2 - DUTY RUNWAY 
 
2.1 
Runway in Use 
 
2.1.1 The preferred runway is RWY 15 for arrivals and departures. Subang Tower shall 
coordinate with Lumpur Approach when RWY 33 needs to be used. 
 
2.2 
Surface Wind Limitation 
 
2.2.1 If the surface wind for the nominated runway registers a tailwind component of 10 
knots or less, operation is still permitted on that runway. 
 
2.2.2 If the tailwind component is in excess of 10 knots, ATC shall advise the flight crew 
of the surface wind and let the flight crews decide on whether to: 
a) continue with the approach. 
b) request for an alternate runway; or 
c) hold for the wind to settle down to 10 knots and below. 
 
2.3 
Reciprocal Runway 
 
2.3.1 The use of reciprocal runway is permitted provided timely coordination is affected. 
Departures are not allowed after the arriving aircraft is less than 20 track miles

c) hold for the wind to settle down to 10 knots and below. 
 
2.3 
Reciprocal Runway 
 
2.3.1 The use of reciprocal runway is permitted provided timely coordination is affected. 
Departures are not allowed after the arriving aircraft is less than 20 track miles 
from touchdown on the reciprocal runway.

SECTION 3 – CHANGE OF RUNWAY PROCEDURES 
 
3.1 
Subang ADC shall coordinate with Lumpur Approach to effect the runway change 
when the need arises. 
 
3.2 
Subang ADC shall advise Lumpur Approach: 
a) the callsign and ETD of the last planned departure for the current runway. 
b) the callsign and ETD of the first planned departure for the new elected runway. 
 
3.3 
Lumpur Approach shall advise Subang ADC: 
a) the callsign and ETA of the last planned arrival for the current runway. 
b) the callsign and ETA of the first planned arrival for the new elected runway.

SECTION 5 – AUTO LAUNCH 
 
5.1 
Auto Launch Procedure 
 
 
a) Only for RWY 15 when mode of operation at KLIA is on RWY 32/33 
configuration. For reciprocal RWY 33 departure, Subang Tower still requires a 
‘Next-Off’ clearance from Lumpur Approach. 
 
b) Spacing between departures minimum of 3 minutes with same performance or 
following is slower succeeding aircraft. 
 
c) If succeeding traffic is faster, Subang ADC shall observe the last vacated 
altitude of the preceding aircraft, establish adequate vertical separation before 
launching the following traffic. 
 
d) Northeast direction – departures from RWY15 making a left turn, Subang Tower 
shall transfer the departure to NEH (118.65 MHz). 
 
e) Southerly direction – departures from RWY15 making a right turn shall be 
transferred by Subang Tower to NWH (124.2 MHz). 
 
f) North / North West direction - departures from RWY15 making a right turn shall 
be transferred by Subang Tower to NWH. 
 
g) Subang ADC should be aware of the new missed approach procedure. Aircraft 
carrying out a missed approach may not be separated with aircraft holding at 
downwind or west of the airfield. 
 
h) Subang ADC shall manage any conflicts or coordinate with Lumpur Approach 
for a non-standard missed approach manoeuvre.

5.3 
Suspension of Auto Launch 
 
When traffic warrants due to the following reasons, Lumpur Approach will inform 
Subang Tower to temporarily suspend the auto launch: 
a) Bad weather with too many aircraft deviating. 
b) Heavy workload at Approach Sector. 
c) Degrading in communication or surveillance facilities. 
d) Deemed appropriate by Approach when circumstances warrant. 
 
Note: Lumpur Approach may stagger the auto launch to more than 3 minutes apart before 
opting to full suspension. Lumpur Approach shall advise Subang Tower in a timely manner 
when auto launch RWY 15 can be resumed.

8.1 
Introduction 
VFR arrivals and departures shall normally be confined to VFR routes. 
Coordination shall be affected between the towers at KLIA, Subang, and KL FIC. 
On a case-by-case basis, VFR flights may be allowed to operate outside the VFR 
routes.

VFR Routes

d) VFR Route 2A Slim River to Seremban – by KL FIC

f) Helicopter access lanes – Lumpur Tower 
g) Subang Eastern (Route Nibong Gila – Batu Caves, up to Bukit Lanjan only) and

8.2.3 Only helicopter flights are approved to operate VFR at KLIA

SECTION 11 - PROVISION OF ASSISTANCE TO VFR TRAFFIC THAT 
ENCOUNTER NAVIGATIONAL DIFFICULTIES AND ARE 
LOST 
 
11.1 
Introduction 
 
VFR traffic may encounter navigational difficulties and may be lost in both in visual 
meteorological conditions or instrument meteorological conditions. It would be 
impossible to predict the precise the nature of response from air traffic control as 
the actual situations in each scenario may vary. 
 
11.2 
Guideline 
 
The following is a general guideline to help an air traffic controller makes the 
appropriate decision in handling such an abnormal situation. 
 
a) Classification 
VFR traffic that is lost shall be classified as aircraft in difficulty or under 
emergency based on the judgment of the air traffic controller and is dependent 
on the situation. 
 
b) Aircraft in difficulty 
A pilot may still be in normal control of his aircraft and able to follow ATC 
instructions or advisory to regain navigational capability with the assistance of

emergency based on the judgment of the air traffic controller and is dependent 
on the situation. 
 
b) Aircraft in difficulty 
A pilot may still be in normal control of his aircraft and able to follow ATC 
instructions or advisory to regain navigational capability with the assistance of 
ATC such as radar vectors while maintaining safe altitudes. This may be 
considered as an aircraft in difficulty until recovery of navigational 
independence. 
 
c) Aircraft under emergency 
VFR traffic in difficult weather, below safe altitudes which affect safe flight may 
be considered as an aircraft in emergency. Aircraft and occupants may be

assistance. 
 
d) Recognition 
Due to workload and other in-flight situations, pilot may forget to declare PAN 
or MAYDAY. Despite this, other verbal commentaries by pilot may indicate that 
he may be facing a difficult situation. It is important that controllers recognize 
the situations as early as possible to provide the necessary assistance. A query 
from the controller to the pilot if he intends to declare a PAN or MAYDAY may 
help clarify the situation for both pilot and controller. 
 
e) Coordination 
Coordination with other relevant units for assistance requires accurate 
communications of the situation. Inaccurate choice of words describing the 
scenario and the type of assistance required may elicit the wrong response and 
mishandling of the situation. Use of the key words such as ‘aircraft in difficulty’ 
or ‘emergency’ will elicit an urgent response rather than the words such as 
‘requesting’, ‘require assistance’. The words request ‘IFR’ and request ‘radar 
vectors’ carry different meaning and circumstances. 
 
f) Priority 
Priority handling of aircraft in difficulty must be recognized and enforced to 
prevent deterioration of the situation. This includes ignoring non-priority

vectors’ carry different meaning and circumstances. 
 
f) Priority 
Priority handling of aircraft in difficulty must be recognized and enforced to 
prevent deterioration of the situation. This includes ignoring non-priority 
coordination, curbing non-priority transmissions, transfer of non-priority traffic 
to adjacent units and when possible, calling for assistance from other ATC 
personnel. 
 
g) Frequency 
In-flight situation sometimes can prevent emergency aircraft from switching 
frequencies to other units. In such circumstance’s controllers, should explore 
the possibility of maintaining traffic concerned on the current frequency and 
relaying the necessary instructions. 
 
h) Confidence building 
In-flight situation of aircraft in difficulty or emergency can be one of stress and 
despair. An accommodating and helpful voice and will help smooth the rough 
situation and build confidence instead of irritated commands and scolding by 
air traffic controllers.

i) Radar Vector Assistance 
MATS Volume 1 Part 8 authorizes controllers to vector VFR aircraft provided 
the aircraft request it or it is suggested by the controller and the aircraft accepts 
it. When vectoring VFR aircraft controllers shall take into consideration the 
surrounding terrain near the aircraft concerned before assigning or suggesting 
an altitude. This includes prevailing weather conditions so as to avoid heading 
the aircraft into IMC. Controllers shall exercise caution when vectoring a VFR 
aircraft as the pilot may be inexperienced and be confused easily.

SECTION 15 - MISSED APPROACH PROCEDURE 
 
15.1 
Runway 15 
 
15.1.1 ILS or LOC Approach & NDB Approach 
Proceed on track 149o climbing initially to 2000ft. Passing 1000ft, not before 15.8 
NM VBA DME, turn right (IAS MAX 210 KT) on TR 320°. Crossing RDL 195 VBA 
continue climb to 3000 ft; reaching 3000 ft turn left bound to RUKVU M.A. Holding 
pattern. 
 
15.1.2 RNAV (GNSS) Approach 
Climb to 2000ft, proceed to SA402 on TR149°, at SA402 (1500ft or above) turn 
right (IAS max 210kt) to SA403 (maintain 2000ft), at SA403 turn right to SA404, at 
SA404 climb to 3000ft proceed to SA405 (maintain 3000ft), at SA405 turn left to 
RUKVU or as directed by ATC. 
 
15.2 
Runway 33 
 
15.2.1 RNAV (GNSS) Approach 
At missed approach point / OCA, climb to 3300ft, proceed to CE (maintain 3300ft) 
on TR329° or as directed by ATC. 
 
Note: Subang ADC should aware that aircraft carrying out a missed approach may not be separated 
with aircraft holding at downwind or west of the airfield 
 
15.3 
Go Around 
On becoming aware of, or initiating a ‘go around’, Subang ADC is to: 
a) Inform, by use of the HOT LINE, the APP controller responsible for providing a 
departure that a missed approach has occurred; 
b) Coordinate with the APP controller to establish separation with any conflicting 
traffic.

several factors, e.g., the distance to touchdown of the arrival, wake turbulence, 
weather conditions, the departing aircraft type, the track after take-off, the flight 
crew, etc.

CHAPTER 4 - EMERGENCY PROCEDURES 
SECTION 1 - GENERAL 
1.1 
Objective 
1.1.1 Emergency procedures are designed to ensure effective coordination amongst 
participating authorities in responding to an aircraft emergency occurring at the 
airport or in its vicinity. The objective is to minimize the effects of an emergency, 
particular in respect of saving lives and maintaining aircraft operation. 
 
1.2

agencies: 
a) Malaysia Airports Sdn Bhd (MASB)

Tengku Ampuan Rahimah / Hospital Besar Kuala Lumpur)

1.4 
Site of Emergency 
 
 
a) Aircraft Crash on Airport 
Aircraft incident/accident in the Critical Rescue and Fire Fighting Access Area 
(CRFFAA) which is a rectangular area surrounding the runway. Its width extends 
150m outward each side of the runway centerline, and its length 1000m beyond 
each threshold. 
b) Aircraft Crash off Airport 
Aircraft incident/accident in the area outside the aerodrome perimeter within a 
distance of approximately 8km (5NM) from the centre of the airport. Aircraft 
crash off airport also includes aircraft incident/accident in the area beyond the 
distance of 8km from the centre of the airport. 
 
1.5 
Degree of Response 
The degree of response by Emergency Services is dependent on the category of 
the emergency. The categories of emergency include: 
a) Aircraft in difficulty – Local standby. 
b) Full Emergency – Imminent Crash. 
c) Full Emergency – Land Crash. 
d) Bomb Threat to aircraft

1.5

the emergency. The categories of emergency include: 
a) Aircraft in difficulty – Local standby. 
b) Full Emergency – Imminent Crash.

1.6 
Initial Action 
 
 
1.6.1 
If an aircraft emergency is detected, air traffic control, or the first person becoming 
aware of the situation shall initiate the applicable procedure. 
1.6.2 
An emergency phase may be upgraded at the discretion of Duty Controller or the 
AFRS Officer-In-Charge as and when the need arises.

SECTION 2 - TYPE OF EMERGENCY AND DEFINITION 
 
There are three types of Aircraft Emergency phase, classified as follows: 
a) Aircraft In Difficulty – Local Standby 
An aircraft in flight known or suspected to have developed some defect but the 
trouble is not such as would normally involve any serious difficulty in effecting a 
safe landing. 
 
b) Full Emergency – Imminent Crash 
An aircraft in flight known or suspected to be in difficulty which may result in a 
force landing or crash on or in the vicinity of the aerodrome. 
 
c) Full Emergency – Land Crash 
Aircraft crash with or without fire which has occurred on or in the vicinity of the 
aerodrome over land.

SECTION 5 - BOMB THREAT TO AIRCRAFT 
 
5.1 
General 
5.1.1 A bomb threat situation exists when information is received alleging that an 
explosive device has been or will be placed on board an aircraft. 
 
5.1.2 Usually, threats from the public are received by telephone and seldom by written 
message or through personal contacts. In most cases threats are delivered 
anonymously. 
 
5.2 
Threat Classification 
All threats shall be treated as genuine until the Airport Evaluation Committee has 
classified them as NON – SPECIFIC (HOAX) or SPECIFIC (GENUINE). 
 
5.2.1 
Non – Specific (Hoax) 
A threat can be classified as HOAX if it does not consist of any or combination 
of these information: 
a) The identification of the airline. 
b) The flight number. 
c) Date and time. 
d) Point or origin or destination. 
e) Location of the bomb. 
 
 
5.2.2 
Specific Threat (Genuine). 
A threat is classified as Genuine Threat when it consists of any one or a 
combination of the following information: 
a) The originator of the threats identifies himself. 
b) The airline is identified.

e) Location of the bomb. 
 
 
5.2.2 
Specific Threat (Genuine). 
A threat is classified as Genuine Threat when it consists of any one or a 
combination of the following information: 
a) The originator of the threats identifies himself. 
b) The airline is identified. 
c) A specific airline / flight is mentioned. 
d) Exact date and / or time is stated.

d) If the aircraft commander advises his intention of landing at another aerodrome,

SECTION 6 - AIRCRAFT HIJACK 
 
6.1 
Unlawful Seizure 
The “Unlawful Seizure of an aircraft” is an act of air piracy and it’s a violation of 
both Malaysian and International Laws. 
 
6.2 
Airborne Seizure 
a) An aircraft that has been hijacked at some point between take-off and landing 
or has been seized on the ground at another airport either locally or abroad, and 
is airborne at the time it was unlawfully seized. 
 
b) Indication of the occurrence of an unlawful seizure of an aircraft in flight is 
normally transmitted to Air Traffic Controllers by the pilot of the seized aircraft 
by means of coded signal, i.e. Transponder Code of 7500. 
 
6.3 
Designated Aircraft Isolated Area. 
 
 
6.3.1 
It is important that action to be taken to isolate the hijacked aircraft. To permit 
isolation of the aircraft, the airport authority (MAB) shall designate an isolated 
parking position at the aerodrome to which such aircraft may be moved 
immediately. 
 
6.3.2 
The Designated Aircraft Isolated Area should be a minimum of 100 m (328 ft) away 
from any other aircraft parking position, runway, building, public area, fuel tank or 
storage area for explosive or incendiary material. 
 
6.3.3 
Care must be taken to ensure that the Designated Aircraft Isolated Area does not

from any other aircraft parking position, runway, building, public area, fuel tank or 
storage area for explosive or incendiary material. 
 
6.3.3 
Care must be taken to ensure that the Designated Aircraft Isolated Area does not 
have gas pipelines, refuelling hydrants, other fuel lines or electric power cable 
beneath the surface. 
 
Note: At present, taxiway J Runway 15 has been designated as an Isolated Aircraft 
Parking Position for aircraft on hijacks or bomb threat.

6.4 
Actions to be taken by Duty Air Traffic Controller: 
 
 
a) To inform all concerned immediately it is known, observed or suspected that an 
aircraft has been hijacked. Refer Appendix A. 
b) To maintain an ongoing communication link with the seized aircraft. 
c) To maintain all normal flight operations. 
d) To make preparation for landing of the seized aircraft.

f) To preserve all audiotapes and other recorded information after the emergency

SECTION 7 RADIO COMMUNICATION FAILURE FOR SULTAN ABDUL AZIZ 
SHAH AIRPORT, SUBANG. 
 
7.1 
If total radio communication failure occurs to an aircraft bound for the Sultan Abdul 
Aziz Shah Airport, Subang, before entering the Kuala Lumpur FIR or entering the 
FIR but before being given or acknowledging a specific STAR, the pilot-in- 
command shall: 
a) In VMC, during daylight hours, maintain VFR and land at Sultan Abdul Aziz 
Shah Airport, Subang or at a suitable aerodrome. Pilot shall take note that the 
KL International Airport is not to be considered as a suitable aerodrome for this 
purpose 
b) In IMC, or between the hours of sunset and sunrise, proceed via flight plan 
route or as cleared by ATC at last assigned level: 
i) If route terminates at VKL, then from VKL proceed to VBA maintaining the 
last assigned flight level; 
ii) If route terminates at VBA, then proceed to step 7.1, d) 
c) Transmit blind position reports and intentions if the aircraft’s transmitter is 
presumed serviceable; 
d) Commence descent in the VBA hold at, or as close as possible to, the EAT last 
received and acknowledged or, if no EAT has been received and 
acknowledged, at or as close as possible to the EAT calculated from the current 
flight plan; 
e) Carry out an instrument approach procedure for Subang runway 15;

2.4 
Wind Indicator and Runway Visual Range (WRVR) 
 
2.4.1 Introduction 
 
WRVR is an automated system providing accurate wind and runway visual range 
data by using intelligent sensor to Selangor Meteorology office and Subang Tower. 
It consists of a set of wind and visibility sensor and installed at the end of runway. 
The weather data captured by the sensors will be transmitted through wireless 
network to the Selangor Meteorology office for data processing. The derived 
information will then be made accessible to Subang Tower via internet through a 
web browser. All the data generated will be transmitted to National Aeronautical 
Meteorology Centre (NAMC).

f) Cloud. ........... (only cloud with base at or below 6500ft shall be included) 
g) Temperature............ 
h) Dew Point............ 
i) QNH............... 
j) Other information.............

Introduction 
 
This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that 
provides guidance and standards for the provision of air traffic services. The ANSM is ANSD 
internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1. 
The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective. 
Throughout this MATS Volume 1, the use of masculine pronouns should be understood to 
represent male and female persons.

Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 1 - General, Issue 
02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 1 - General shall be read together with 
Civil Aviation Regulations 2016, Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 1, CAD 2, CAD 11, 
CAD 1101, CAD 12 and CAD 1007. 
1.2

The MATS Volume 1, Part 1 - General contains standard operating procedures, 
act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other operational personnel 
tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their area of responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3

This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026.

General Administration  
2.1 
Introduction 
 
Aircraft operations in Malaysia are regulated in accordance with the Civil Aviation 
Act (CAA) 1969 and Civil Aviation Regulations (CAR) 2016. The Chief Executive 
Officer (CEO) of Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM) assumes overall 
responsibility for promoting the safety and efficiency of civil aviation in Malaysia in 
accordance with the CAA 1969, CAR 2016, CADs, Civil Aviation Guidance 
Materials, CAAM Act 2017 and Civil Aviation (Amendment) Regulations 2018. He 
advises the Government on all policy matters concerning international civil aviation 
including those pertaining to the provision of air traffic services. As a contracting 
state to International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), air traffic services within 
the airspace under the control of Malaysia are provided in conformity with the 
ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices. 
 
To meet the objectives of safety and efficiency of aircraft operations within the 
airspace controlled by Malaysia, 2 Flight Information Regions (FIRs), namely, the 
Kuala Lumpur and Kota Kinabalu FIRs have been established. Within each of 
these FIRs, ATSUs have been established to provide appropriate area control 
service, approach control service, aerodrome control service, flight information
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 1 - GENERAL (03072026).pdf

text:
Kuala Lumpur and Kota Kinabalu FIRs have been established. Within each of 
these FIRs, ATSUs have been established to provide appropriate area control 
service, approach control service, aerodrome control service, flight information 
service and alerting service. These services are provided, as appropriate, from 
airport control towers and air traffic control centres (ATCCs). 
 
To enable the military to meet its national requirements, a number of control zones, 
training areas, and danger areas have been established, and operational control 
of these airspaces and responsibility for the provision of ATS within these 
airspaces have been delegated to the military.  
 
The Director of ANSOD, Regional Director Peninsular/Sabah/Sarawak are 
responsible to the Deputy CEO (Operations) acting under the authority of the CEO, 
are the authorities responsible for the overall administration of ATS in the provision 
of ATS within the Kuala Lumpur and Kota Kinabalu FIRs. The CAAM Organisation 
Chart is depicted in Appendix 4.

aware by reason of their employment unless authorised by the CEO.

Daily Operation Briefing shall be prepared by the HOW Watch Manager/Watch 
Supervisor/Tower Supervisor using a standard template as provided in Part 18, 
Appendix 1. 
 
As part of the briefing, air traffic controllers are encouraged to utilise the time for 
orderly hand-over/take-over before a shift start, or to enable opening/closing checks 
to be completed. 
 
The Importance of briefing are:  
 Safety: To share critical information about weather conditions, airfield status 
and airspace activities to ensure the safety of all aircraft under AOR. 
 Communication, Navigation, Surveillance and ATM System Status: To 
update on the status of equipment and systems to avoid any service 
disruptions or degraded performance that could impact their ability to manage 
air traffic. 
 
Situational Awareness: To ensure Air Traffic Control Officers (ATCOs) are 
aware of the current traffic situation, including any ongoing or upcoming 
critical events to assist in decision making and effectively respond to 
unexpected situations. 
 Abnormal Situations: To help ATCOs to respond swiftly and efficiently in 
case of any unexpected emergencies in the future through debriefing 
sessions. Debriefing could include discussions about emergency procedures 
and contingency plans.

2.4 
Guideline for Handover Watch (HOW) And Takeover Watch (TOW) Procedures  
 
In an ATC operational environment, the handover and takeover watch process is 
a standard but safety-critical task that needs to be completed thoroughly and 
accurately. It is to ensure that the incoming (takeover) controller will acquire an 
adequate overview not only of the traffic situation but also of the control strategies 
of the outgoing (handover) controller.

Handover-Takeover Basic Principles 
 
ATCs shall adopt four basics principles during HOW-TOW: 
 Handover commences in a “clean” situation, (i.e., there is no emergency 
or abnormal situation developing and the conflicts are either solved or a 
plan to resolve has been made); 
 The takeover (incoming) controller shall arrive earlier and the handover 
(outgoing) controller shall remain near the working position until he/she is 
certain that the situational awareness of the incoming controller is at a 
desired level; 
 
A HOW-TOW Quick Reference in the form of a checklist shall be used as 
a guideline so that any vital information is not neglected or omitted; and 
 Both controllers shall sign the HOW-TOW Quick Reference to 
acknowledge all information given/relay by the handover controller. 
 
The Handover/Takeover Watch shall: 
 Be conducted at a distance that both controllers should be able to listen 
attentively to each other;  
 Be in a two-way, with both controllers taking joint responsibility to ensure 
the exchange of accurate information and effective communication takes 
place; 
 
Use verbal and written means of communication; 
 Be accommodated as much time as necessary to complete the process; 
and 
 Be conducted by rated working controllers and not by a trainee or someone 
else, except for training purposes.

comfortable duration to ensure the incoming controller has assimilated all the 
essential information and acquired total awareness of the situation as required.

All controllers shall be prohibited from using mobile phones and other electronic 
devices in operational areas of control towers and ATCCs, except for situations as 
described in paragraph 2.8.3, including:  
 Live streaming, recording, uploading, and disseminating video, audio, and 
visual content related to air traffic control operations without consent from the 
CEO, and 
 Using of mobile phones while providing ATS. 
 
The prohibition of using mobile phones and other electronic devices in the 
operational areas is to protect and enhance the working environment in order to 
maintain an efficient and safe operation at the control towers and ATCCs from: 
 Distraction: Mobile phones and other electronic devices can distract 
controllers from their critical duties of monitoring and managing air traffic. 
Engaging with personal calls, messages, or apps can divert attention away 
from crucial tasks, leading to errors or delays in communication and decision-
making; 
 Potential for Human Error: When a controller uses mobile phone or electronic 
devices while performing critical duties, such as issuing instructions to pilots 
or coordinating aircraft movements, it could inadvertently lead to human error 
and may create "holes" in Swiss Cheese model, thus contribute to incidents 
or accidents; and

Security Risks: Mobile phones and other electronic devices may pose security 
risks if they are used to transmit sensitive information or if they are

systems or communication networks through a mobile device could 
jeopardize aviation safety and national security. 
 
Recognizing the varied nature of work and the unpredictability of certain situations,

 Usage of mobile phones for work-related calls and messages if the matter is 
urgent and cannot be delayed until the end of the work period; or 
 In the event of a genuine emergency where immediate communication is 
required, controllers are permitted to use their mobile phones. 
 
However, it is expected that such usage in paragraph 2.8.3 will be kept to the 
minimum required time and should be reported to the immediate supervisor as

entries of concern to them, which were made during the period since their last tour 
of duty before accepting responsibility for an operating position.

annotated to enable him to take follow-up action.

with exact times. As soon as possible thereafter, a detailed entry shall be made in 
the log.

The ILS inspection may take between 1.5 to 2 hours to assess the localizer 
(LOC) course alignment, glide path (GP) angular alignment, marker operation 
and alarm settings.  
 
The flight inspection aircraft shall execute nine different profiles, in order to 
complete the ILS inspection, and some profiles may be repeated. The 
descriptions of each profile are stated below: 
 Profile 01 - Centreline (Descending Run Down to 50 ft) 
1) The purpose is to check the LOC course, GP slope and alarms.  
2) The flight inspection aircraft will position itself along the extended 
runway centreline, at a distance and height to be coordinated with 
ATC, and commence its run inbound towards the LOC antenna. 
3) On capturing the GP at approximately 5 NM out, it will commence 
descend towards the threshold down to 50 ft AGL irrespective of 
whether the facility is CAT I or CAT II. 
4) As soon as the 50 ft AGL point is reached, the pilot of the flight 
inspection aircraft will overshoot the runway, and indicate to ATC a left 
or right turn to position for next inspection profile.

4.14 
ATC Procedure 
 
Aircraft will acknowledge receipt of the ATIS by referring to the message code on 
initial contact with Area or Approach Control (arriving aircraft) or Aerodrome 
Control (departing aircraft). If an aircraft acknowledges receipt of an ATIS 
broadcast that is no longer current, controllers shall transmit without delay to the 
aircraft any element of information that has been updated. 
 
When rapidly changing weather conditions make it impracticable to include 
weather reports in the broadcast, the ATIS message is to indicate that the relevant 
information will be passed on to RTF by ATC. 
 
Prior to transmission, the data should be recorded in an ATIS form and the 
message verified for accuracy. The time the message recording was completed 
should be entered in the form. Prior to actual transmission, the recorded messages 
shall be verified. The ATIS forms shall be retained for a specified period in 
accordance with unit instructions. 
 
Each operating position at the control tower shall be given a copy of the broadcast 
unless an automatic display of such information is available. ATSUs shall establish 
UOIs specifying the distribution and acknowledgement of ATIS messages at other 
operating positions concerned.

General 
 
An ILS system essentially consists of the following sub-systems: 
 The VHF Localiser (LOC) sub-system to give course guidance;  
 The UHF Glidepath (GP) system to give final descent guidance;  
 
Outer Marker (OM) and Middle Marker (MM) for position fixing;  
 DME associated with the GP for distance guidance to touchdown if markers 
are impractical;  
 Uninterrupted power supply system (UPS);  
 
Remote monitoring system; and  
 System identification signal in two or three alphabets, for example: IKL.

CAT II Operations 
 
All weather ILS Category II (and III) operations are based on a total system 
concept. The system requires additional and more reliable ground equipment and 
airborne systems capable of guiding the aircraft with greater accuracy to the 
decision height and, when appropriate through a landing and subsequent roll-off. 
The pilot is part of the system and takes an active role in the operation. 
 
When Category II operations are in progress, controllers shall ensure that aircraft 
do not take-off from the same runway after an aircraft on final approach has 
descended to 200 ft (60 m), as the departing aircraft will cause interference to the 
localiser beam when it flies over the localiser antenna. For this same reason, 
controllers should increase the intervals between successive landing aircraft. 
 
As Category II operations are inherently more critical especially if very poor 
visibility conditions prevail, controllers shall notify pilots immediately of any 
changes to the operational status of the associated ground systems (e.g., failure 
of the ILS or approach lights) or, meteorological occurrence (e.g., wind shear) or 
which is operationally relevant, to enable the pilot to decide whether to continue 
or abandon the approach.

General

basic tool which enables controllers to visualise the disposition of traffic within 
their area of responsibility including traffic arriving and departing an aerodrome, 
assess conflicts and control aircraft in a safe manner. 
 
 To assist in the visualisation, the FPS are displayed on a flight progress board 
(FPB). The FPB is generally laid out so that the top of the FPB represents North. 
The FPB has a number of bays in which key reporting points/airports (FPB 
designators) are positioned. The designators, which serve as conflict 
assessment points, are generally displayed as follows:  
 In accordance with their geographical relationship to the extent practicable 
within a sector’s airspace; and  
 As the FAF and the first departure point for approach and aerodrome 
positions. 
 
The FPS are displayed on the FPB below the associated FPB designators and 
manipulated in accordance with the progress of flight.

Controller Working Positions Combined Procedure  
 
Recognising the importance of operational efficiency and safety in the dynamic 
field of air traffic services, there is a need of combining controller working positions 
depending on traffic volume and complexity of the control area to meet varying 
operational demands.  
 
This procedure is intended to serve as a guideline for combining controller working 
positions with the optimal use of manpower and resources.  
 
The purposes of this procedure are to: 
 Define the factors to be considered when combining controller working 
positions; and 
 Describe the procedures on combining controller working positions. 
 
Factors to be considered for combining controller working positions without 
compromising safety includes, but not limited to:   
 The Area of Responsibility (AOR) continues to have reliable radio frequency 
coverage after the combination; 
 Combination of the Controller Working Position (CWP) is feasible;  
 
Configuration of controller working positions depending on the traffic volume 
and anticipated workload;   
 Station’s staff strength is not capable of fulfilling the manpower required to 
operate in normal working positions; or  
 During the activation of Business Continuity Plan (BCP).

Introduction 
 
This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that 
provides guidance and standards for the provision of air traffic services. The ANSM is ANSD 
internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1. 
The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective. 
Throughout this MATS Volume 1, the use of masculine pronouns should be understood to 
represent male and female persons.

1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 10 - Coordination, Issue 
02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 10 - Coordination shall be read together 
with Civil Aviation Regulation 2016, International Civil Aviation Organization Doc 
4444, Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 1, CAD 2, CAD 11, CAD 12, CAD 1007 and 
CAD 1101. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 10 - Coordination contains standard operating 
procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other operational 
personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their area of 
responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026.

2.1 
General 
 
The coordination and transfer of control of a flight between successive Air Traffic 
Services Units (ATSUs) and control sectors shall be affected by a dialogue 
comprising the following stages: 
 Notification of the flight in order to prepare for coordination, as necessary; 
 Coordination of conditions of transfer of control by the transferring ATSU; 
 
Coordination, if necessary, and acceptance of conditions of transfer of control 
by the accepting ATSU; and 
 The transfer of control to the accepting ATSU or control sector. 
 
With approval by the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), ANSD is responsible for the 
establishment of Operational Letters of Agreement (OLOA)/Air Traffic Services 
Coordination Procedures (ATSCP) defining the procedures, release of airspace if 
any for operational purposes, and the communications requirements to ensure the 
safe and expeditious movement of flights operating between or transiting the Flight 
Information Regions (FIRs). 
 
ATSUs should, to the extent possible, establish and apply standardised 
procedures for the coordination and transfer of control of flights, in order, inter alia, 
to reduce the need for verbal coordination. Such coordination procedures shall

2.2 
Coordination Between ATSUs Providing ATS Within Contiguous Control Areas 
 
General 
 ATSUs shall forward from unit to unit, as the flight progresses, necessary flight 
plan and control information. When so required by the agreement between 
the appropriate ATS authorities to assist in the separation of aircraft, flight 
plan and flight progress information for flights along specified routes or 
portions of routes in close proximity to FIR boundaries shall also be provided 
to the ATSUs in charge of the FIR adjacent to such routes or portions of 
routes. 
Note1. - Such a route or portion of route is often referred to as an area of common 
interest, the extent of which is usually determined by the required separation 
minima. 
Note2. - See also Chapter 3 - Coordination in Respect of The Provision of Flight 
Information Service and Alerting Service. 
 The flight plan and control information shall be transmitted in sufficient time to

text:
interest, the extent of which is usually determined by the required separation 
minima. 
Note2. - See also Chapter 3 - Coordination in Respect of The Provision of Flight 
Information Service and Alerting Service. 
 The flight plan and control information shall be transmitted in sufficient time to 
permit reception and analysis of the data by the receiving unit(s) and the 
necessary coordination between the units concerned. 
 
Transfer of Control 
 The responsibility for the control of an aircraft shall be transferred from the 
ATSU to the next unit at the time of crossing the common control area 
boundary as determined by the unit having control of the aircraft or at such 
other point or time as has been agreed between the two units. 
 Where specified in OLOA/ATSCP between the ATSUs concerned, and when 
transferring an aircraft, the transferring unit shall notify the accepting unit that 
the aircraft is in position to be transferred, and specify that the responsibility 
for control should be assumed by the accepting unit forthwith at the time of 
crossing the control boundary or other transfer control point specified in letters 
of agreement between the ATSUs or at such other point or time coordinated 
between the two units.

 Coordination Environments  
 
Air Traffic Control (ATC) procedures vary significantly, depending on the 
surveillance capabilities of the coordinating ATSUs in a given boundary 
environment. For the purpose of this subchapter the coordination environments 
are identified as either surveillance or procedural. In some instances, the same 
type of message may require the inclusion of different or additional data to 
accommodate the demands of differing environments. Depending on the

accommodate the demands of differing environments. Depending on the 
environment, the timing of the transmission of these messages may also vary. 
The environment may also affect whether the AIDC message is automatically 
processed, or displayed to the controller for manual processing.  
 
A surveillance environment is an environment where an ATS surveillance 
system is in use, and allows controllers to positively identify the traffic. Radar 
and/or Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast (ADS-B) are available to 
the controllers at sector positions on both sides of a common boundary, and 
traffic is identified by information presented on a situation display. Such facilities 
permit surveillance coordination procedures to be used.  
 
 A procedural environment exists in those areas where surveillance 
coordination procedures are not available because at least one of the 
coordinating ATSUs does not have a surveillance capability, or the surveillance 
capabilities differ. For example, surveillance in oceanic and remote areas is 
often achieved with Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Contract (ADS-C), 
Controller Pilot Data Link Communications (CPDLC) or voice position reports; 
in such areas, coordination procedures differ from those used in a surveillance 
environment.

General 
 
The arrangements for activities potentially hazardous to civil aircraft, whether over 
the territory of a State or over the high seas, shall be coordinated through the 
CEO. The coordination shall be affected early enough to permit timely 
promulgation of information regarding the activities in accordance with the 
provisions of CAD 15. 
 
If CAAM is not that of the State where the organisation planning the activities 
is located, initial coordination should be affected through the CEO responsible 
for the airspace over the State where the organisation is located. 
 
The objective of the coordination shall be to achieve the best arrangements which 
will avoid hazards to civil aircraft and minimise interference with the normal 
operations of such aircraft. 
 
In determining these arrangements, the following should be applied: 
 the locations or areas, times and durations for the activities should be 
selected to avoid closure or realignment of established ATS routes, 
blocking of the most economic flight levels, or delays of scheduled aircraft 
operations, unless no other options exist; 
 the size of the airspace designated for the conduct of the activities should 
be kept as small as possible;

Runway Visual Range 
 
General 
 
Runway Visual range (RVR) is defined as the range over which the pilot of an 
aircraft on the centreline of a runway can see the runway surface markings or 
the lights delineating the runway or identifying its centreline. RVR is not a 
“measurement” or “observation” of a meteorological parameter such as wind 
direction and speed, temperature or pressure. It is an assessment that takes 
into account a number of factors both atmospheric and non-atmospheric. 
 
The purpose of RVR is to provide pilots, ATSUs and other aeronautical users

into account a number of factors both atmospheric and non-atmospheric. 
 
The purpose of RVR is to provide pilots, ATSUs and other aeronautical users 
with information on runway visibility conditions during periods of low visibility 
caused by fog, etc. Specifically, RVR is required to allow an assessment to be 
made as to whether conditions are above or below the specified operating 
minima. More generally, pilots use the RVR as an indication of the visual 
guidance that may be expected during the final approach, flare, touchdown and 
roll-out.

metres or less and shall be made on all runways intended for use during periods 
of reduced visibility and in particular on:

which are used for take-off.

RVR Observing Techniques 
 
The most frequently used RVR observing techniques are:

Under instrumental techniques, normally transmissometers are installed to 
measure the transmittance of light through unit distance of the atmosphere 
along specified points along a runway. Installation may consist of up to three

processor. The transmissometers may be located one at each end of the 
runway adjacent to the touchdown zone and the third near the runway mid-
point area. For Radio Telephony (RTF) purposes the locations are known as 
“Touchdown”, “Mid-point” and “Stop-end”. Processors automatically compute 
the RVR for each location and display it in digital form to ATC.

Human Observer Technique 
 
This method involves counting the number of runway edge lights that can be 
seen by an observer from the touchdown zone of a runway. The number of 
lights observed is converted into a RVR range using the distance between each 
light and, after making due allowance for differences in light intensity, 
background, etc. For simplicity however, a straight conversion is usually done.  
 
The observation shall preferably be taken standing on a suitable vehicle to 
simulate as far as practicable the cockpit height – usually 5 metres with the 
runway lights normally set at maximum intensity.

Search and Rescue Requirements 
 
RCCs shall maintain close liaison with the MET office to obtain the required 
information for SAR operations. Information required by the RCCs shall include, if

the missing aircraft and along the intended route of the aircraft with particular 
reference to: 
 Significant en route weather phenomena;

bases and tops; 
 
Visibility and phenomena reducing visibility; 
 Surface wind and upper wind; 
 State of ground, in particular, any flooding;

 Sea level pressure data.

 Meteorological information that were supplied to the missing aircraft, e.g.,

Introduction 
 
 The objective of the Aeronautical Information Services (AIS) is to ensure the 
flow of aeronautical data and aeronautical information necessary for global 
ATM system safety, regularity, economy and efficiency in an environmentally 
sustainable manner. The role and importance of aeronautical data and 
aeronautical information changed significantly with the implementation of area 
navigation (RNAV), performance-based navigation (PBN), airborne computer-
based navigation systems, performance-based communication (PBC), 
performance-based surveillance (PBS), data link systems and satellite voice 
communications 
(SATVOICE). 
Corrupt, 
erroneous, 
late, 
or 
missing 
aeronautical data and aeronautical information can potentially affect the safety

scheduled time of operation, and any applicable restrictions or hazards to 
manned aircraft.

General 
1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 11 - Air Traffic Services 
Messages, Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 11 - Air Traffic Services Messages shall 
be read together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 2, CAD 11, International Civil 
Aviation Organization (ICAO) Doc 9683, ICAO Doc 9869 and ICAO Doc 10037. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 11 - Air Traffic Services Messages contains standard 
operating procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other 
operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their 
area of responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026. 
1.4 
Interpretation of Words 
Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil 
Aviation Authority of Malaysia Act 2017 [Act 788]. 
May means the procedure/instruction is permissive, optional or alternative. 
Miles always refers to nautical miles (NM). 
Shall, is to, are to and must means the instruction is mandatory.

Chapter 4 - Methods of Message Exchange 
 
 
 
4-1 
4 
Methods of Message Exchange 
4.1 
General 
 
The lead-time requirements of air traffic control and flow control procedures shall 
determine the method of message exchange to be used for the exchange of ATS 
data. 
 
The method of message exchange shall also be dependent upon the availability 
of adequate communications channels, the function to be performed, the types of 
data to be exchanged and the processing facilities at the centres concerned. 
 
Basic flight plan data necessary for flow control procedures shall be furnished at 
least 60 minutes in advance of the flight. Basic flight plan data shall be provided 
by either a filed flight plan or a repetitive flight plan submitted by mail in the form 
of a repetitive flight plan listing form or other media suitable for electronic data-
processing systems. 
 
Flight plan data submitted in advance of flight shall be updated by time, level and 
route changes and other essential information as may be necessary. 
 
Basic flight plan data necessary for air traffic control purposes shall be furnished 
to the first en route control centre at least 30 minutes in advance of the flight, and 
to each successive centre at least 20 minutes before the aircraft enters that 
centre’s area of jurisdiction, in order for it to prepare for the transfer of control.

(See Sections 1.3 to 1.8 of this Appendix)
 
Composition of the standard types of message 
 
The composition of each standard type of 
message, expressed as a standardized sequence of 
fields of data, shall be as prescribed in the reference 
table on this page. Each message shall contain all the 
fields prescribed. 
 
Composition of the standard types of field 
 
The composition of each standard type of field, 
expressed as a standardised sequence of elements of 
data, or in some cases as a simple element, shall be as 
prescribed in the field tables on pages A3-6 to AP-C-
26. 
 
Note: Each type of field contains at least one 
mandatory element and, except in Field Type 9, this is 
the first or only element in the field. The rules for the 
inclusion or omission of conditional elements are 
indicated in the field tables.

on page copy by an open bracket ‘(’, which constitutes 
the Start-of-ATS-Data Signal. This signal shall be

Data conventions 
 
    
Most of the conventions to be used in the 
expression of ATS data in the messages are prescribed 
in the field tables on pages AP-C-5 to AP-C-26, but 
the conventions for the expression of level, position 
and route data are given below. 
 
The expression of level data 
 
Four alternative conventions are available for the 
expression of level data: 
 
(a) “F” followed by 3 decimal numerics: 
 
indicates a flight level number, i.e. Flight Level 
340 is expressed as “F340”; 
 
(b) “S” followed by 4 decimal numerics: 
indicates standard metric level in tens of metres,

Four alternative conventions are available for the 
expression of level data: 
 
(a) “F” followed by 3 decimal numerics: 
 
indicates a flight level number, i.e. Flight Level 
340 is expressed as “F340”; 
 
(b) “S” followed by 4 decimal numerics: 
indicates standard metric level in tens of metres, 
i.e. Standard Metric Level 11 300 m (Flight Level 
370) is expressed as “S1130”; 
 
(c)  “A” followed by 3 decimal numerics: 
indicates altitude in hundreds of feet, i.e. an 
altitude of 4,500 ft is expressed as “A045”; 
 
(d) “M” followed by 4 decimal numerics: 
indicates altitude in tens of metres, i.e. an altitude 
of 8,400 m is expressed as “M0840”. 
 
The expression of position or route 
 
The following alternative data conventions shall be 
used for the expression of position or route: 
 
(a) from 2 to 7 characters, being the coded 
designator assigned to an ATS route to be flown; 
 
 
b)  from 2 to 5 characters, being the coded designator 
 
assigned to an en route point; 
 
(c)  4 numerics describing latitude in degrees and tens 
 
and units of minutes, followed by “N” (meaning 
 
“North”) or “S” (South), followed by 5 numerics 
 
describing longitude in degrees and tens and units 
 
of minutes, followed by “E” (East) or “W” 
(West). The correct number of numerics is to be 
made up, where necessary, by the insertion of 
zeros, e.g “4620N07805W”; 
 
(d)  2 numerics describing latitude in degrees, 
followed by “N” (North) or “S” (South), followed

text:

(West). The correct number of numerics is to be 
made up, where necessary, by the insertion of 
zeros, e.g “4620N07805W”; 
 
(d)  2 numerics describing latitude in degrees, 
followed by “N” (North) or “S” (South), followed 
by 3 numerics describing longitude in degrees, 
followed by “E” (East) or “W” (West). Again, the 
correct number of numerics is to be made up, 
where necessary, by the insertion of zeros, e.g. 
“46N078W”; 
 
(e)  2 to 5 characters being the coded identification of 
a significant point, followed by 3 decimal 
numerics giving the bearing from the point in 
degrees magnetic followed by 3 decimal numerics 
giving the distance from the point in nautical 
miles. In areas of high latitude where it is 
determined by the appropriate authority that 
reference to degrees magnetic is impractical, 
degrees true may be used. The correct number of 
numerics is to be made up, where necessary, by 
the insertion of zeros, e.g. a point at 180° 
magnetic at a distance of 40 NM from VOR 
“VAS” would be expressed as “VAS180040”.

each type of message to be followed.

 THA402)

This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that 
provides guidance and standards for the provision of air traffic services. The ANSM is ANSD 
internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1. 
The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective.

represent male and female persons.

Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 12 - Phraseologies, 
Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 12 - Phraseologies shall be read 
together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 11, CAD 1101, International Civil 
Aviation Organization (ICAO) Doc 9683, ICAO Doc 9869 and ICAO Doc 10037. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 12 - Phraseologies contains standard operating 
procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other operational 
personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their area of 
responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller.

This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026.

Should means that the procedure or instruction is recommended. It is applied where

2 
General Provisions 
2.1 
Introduction 
 
Precise and unambiguous communications between controllers and pilots and, 
between controllers themselves is extremely important in air traffic service to meet 
the objectives of safety and efficiency. This is all the more important because of 
the diverse nationalities and languages involved. Accordingly, ICAO has 
developed a comprehensive list of phrases, which are designed to be precise and 
concise, for use in air traffic services. 
 
This part lays down the procedures, phraseology and guidance material with the 
objective of ensuring uniformity in telephone and Radio Telephony (RTF) 
communications. 
 
Controllers and other Air Traffic Services (ATS) personnel shall observe the 
highest standard of discipline at all times with respect to the use of the standard 
phraseology given in the MATS. Controllers may, on occasions find it necessary 
to extend or modify the phraseology but in doing so they should take care not to 
deviate from or prejudice basic meanings or intentions. 
 
They are not intended to be exhaustive, and when circumstances differ, pilots, 
ATS personnel and other ground personnel will be expected to use plain language, 
which should be as clear and concise as possible, to the level specified in the 
ICAO language proficiency requirements contained in CAD 1007 - English
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 12 - PHRASEOLOGIES (03072026).pdf

text:
ATS personnel and other ground personnel will be expected to use plain language, 
which should be as clear and concise as possible, to the level specified in the 
ICAO language proficiency requirements contained in CAD 1007 - English 
Language Proficiency Testing (ELPT). 
 
Controllers should avoid: 
 too rapid delivery of instructions especially with pilots who are not fluent in the 
English language; 
 the assumption that visiting pilots are as familiar with the local area and airfield 
as the locally based pilots; 
 
verbosity and excessive use of courtesies; 
 using hesitation syllables such as “er” or “ah” “mmm” etc.; and 
 entering into non-operational conversation with pilots. 
 
Controllers shall not direct transmission to an aircraft during take-off, during the 
last part of the final approach or during the landing roll except for reasons of safety. 
 
During busy periods when simultaneous calls from several aircraft are likely, 
controllers should decide on the order of reply based on the disposition of the 
traffic at that time.

Speech Technique 
 
The correct enunciation of words, spoken at a uniform rate, will do much to assist 
the satisfactory reception of speech through the telephone and radio media 
including HF. In this connection controllers should:

highly directional properties;

the ATS Unit; and 
 
depress the transmit switch fully before speech is commenced and to release 
the switch only after the transmission is completed.

when answering a call on the intercom, telephone system or radio. This will confirm 
to the caller that he is communicating with the right person at the other end.

 “Sector 2” if responding to another work position within the same unit on the 
intercom;

control circuit design built-in, which will automatically adjust signal levels. This

RTF and Intercom Procedures and Techniques 
 
RTF always has priority over intercom or telephones. 
 
When an aircraft calls, the controllers must listen carefully, record and check the 
details of the message and acknowledge immediately. If a pilot requests 
information or a clearance which is not immediately available, the controller must 
acknowledge and advise the pilot to “standby” whilst the required information or 
clearance is obtained. The pilot’s call must not be ignored whilst the information/ 
clearance is being obtained as this will cause the pilot to repeat his requests. 
 
If a controller is coordinating on the intercom when an aircraft calls, he must 
immediately give attention to the pilot’s message and acknowledge before 
proceeding with the intercom call. In such instances, it will be appropriate to say 
“standby” or “call you back” to the person on the intercom. 
 
When replying to aircraft transmissions, controllers shall acknowledge by using 
the aircraft callsign, and NOT by using “Roger”.

The similarity of some aircraft callsigns on the same frequency can cause 
confusion, which could lead to incidents. Controllers should therefore maintain 
strict RTF discipline to prevent confusion. 
 
When there is likelihood that callsigns will be confused, controllers shall warn the 
pilots of the aircraft concerned, especially when the flight numbers are identical, 
e.g., MAS 117 and SIA 117. Controllers shall ensure that they use the full callsign

Controllers shall as a general rule, always use company designators when they 
are part of a callsign.

read back of clearances to avoid any possible confusion.

Information regarding the quality of the aircraft transmission. 
Example: “Malaysian 123, this is Lumpur Tower, reading you five.” 
4.7 
Continuation of Communications 
 
Once satisfactory two-way communications with an aircraft has been established, 
controllers are permitted to shorten the procedures provided that no mistaken 
identity or confusion is likely to arise. 
 
Controllers may assume that the aircraft is listening out and, may transmit 
messages without waiting for a reply from the aircraft. Phrases such as “over”, 
“roger”, “this is” and “out” may be omitted. 
4.8 
Acknowledgement and Read – Back of Messages 
 
RTF loading and traffic density will largely determine the degree of read-back 
which is possible and desirable. As a general principle, all messages shall be 
acknowledged by controllers by the use of the aircraft callsign. 
4.9 
Transfer of Communications 
 
Controllers shall transfer communication with an aircraft to another unit by giving 
the following instructions: 
 The identity of the unit to be contacted; and  
 The frequency to be used for contact.

intermediate 25kHz, the full figure will comprise 6 digits. However, controllers need 
only to pass the first five digits. Example: if the frequency is 124.725 MHz, only 
124.72 be passed.

operational messages to aircraft. The transmission of such messages shall be

Telephone Arrangements 
5.1 
General 
 
While most ATS Units are equipped with Subscriber Trunk Dialling (STD) 
telephones, there may be instances to obtain the services of the telephone 
network provider to connect calls. Three priority categories of call are available to 
ATC and their order of priority are: 
 Distress Call; 
 Lightning Call; 
 
Urgent Call. 
 
The prefix “Distress Call” is reserved for extreme operationally urgent situations or 
when immediate connection is essential because safety of human life is involved. 
“Distress Calls” have absolute priority over all other calls and will be connected 
immediately, other calls being disconnected if necessary. 
 
The prefix “Lightning Call” is strictly reserved for calls relating to operational 
matters which may develop into “Distress” and for most urgent matters of essential 
administrative importance. A “Lightning Call” will be connected ahead of “Urgent” 
and other calls which have been booked. Existing calls will not be disconnected 
for “Lightning Calls” but such calls will be offered to engaged extensions. 
 
The prefix “Urgent Call” is reserved for calls of urgent operational or administrative 
importance. An “Urgent Call” takes precedence over all except “Distress” and 
“Lightning” calls. Existing calls will not be disconnected for “Urgent Calls” such 
calls will be offered to engaged extensions.

2.1 
General 
 
The various circumstances surrounding each emergency situation preclude the 
establishment of exact detailed procedures to be followed. The procedures 
outlined herein are intended as a general guide to air traffic services personnel. 
Air traffic control units shall maintain full and complete coordination, and personnel 
shall use their best judgement in handling emergency situations. 
Note1. - Additional procedures to be applied in relation to emergencies and 
contingencies while using an Air Traffic Services (ATS) surveillance system are 
contained in Part 8, Chapter 9. 
Note2. - If the pilot of an aircraft encountering a state of emergency has previously 
been directed by Air Traffic Control (ATC) to select a specific transponder code 
and/or a specific Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast (ADS-B) 
emergency mode, that code and/or mode will normally be maintained unless, in 
special circumstances, the pilot has decided or has been advised otherwise. 
Where ATC has not requested a code or emergency mode to be set, the pilot will 
set the transponder to Mode A Code 7700 and/or the appropriate ADS-B 
emergency mode. 
Note3. - Some aircraft equipped with first generation ADS-B avionics have the 
capability to transmit a general emergency alert only, regardless of the code 
selected by the pilot.

2.2 
Guidelines 
 
Controllers shall apply the rules and procedures in this section as the basis for 
handling aircraft emergencies. Different circumstances may affect an emergency 
and because of this it is not possible to specify procedures to cover every 
emergency situation. Controllers are therefore expected to use their best 
judgement to assess and handle a situation not specifically covered in this manual. 
 
If circumstances dictate, controllers may vary the standard radiotelephony 
phraseology and procedures to handle an emergency situation. However, 
controllers shall always bear in mind the need to be precise and, to take into 
consideration aircrew workload during emergencies.

Emergency Separation 
 
If, during an emergency situation, it is not possible to ensure that the applicable 
horizontal separation can be maintained, emergency separation of half the 
applicable vertical separation minimum may be used, i.e., 500 ft (150 m) between 
aircraft in airspace where a vertical separation minimum of 1,000 ft (300 m) is 
applied, and 300 m (1,000 ft) between aircraft in airspace where a 2,000 ft (600 
m) vertical separation minimum is applied.

advised that emergency separation is being applied and informed of the actual 
minimum used. Additionally, all flight crews concerned shall be provided with 
essential traffic information.

those applicable to non-ACAS equipped aircraft. In particular, the prevention of

assumed collision, enables the pilot to identify the conflicting traffic and, if 
necessary, take avoiding action. Warnings by ACAS II equipped aircraft are given

Autonomous Distress Tracking of Aircraft in Flight as Part of The ICAO 
Aeronautical Distress and Safety System 
 
The ICAO established the Global Aeronautical Distress and Safety System 
(GADSS) to address challenges in the global air navigation system concerning 
the timely identification and localisation of aircraft in distress, including lessons 
learned from accidents such as Air France flight AF447 and Malaysia Airlines 
flight MH370.  
 
GADSS provides a globally consistent approach to enhancing the alerting 
procedures of SAR services, comprises three (3) main elements:  
 
Aircraft tracking; 
 
Location of an aircraft in distress through Autonomous Distress Tracking 
(ADT); and 
 
Post-flight localisation and recovery (PFLR). 
 
Through these elements, GADSS enhances the availability of aircraft position

text:
Aircraft tracking; 
 
Location of an aircraft in distress through Autonomous Distress Tracking 
(ADT); and 
 
Post-flight localisation and recovery (PFLR). 
 
Through these elements, GADSS enhances the availability of aircraft position 
information in abnormal situations (i.e. crash, forced landing, or ditching) and 
supports timely SAR response through improved availability of information on 
the location of the survivors, aircraft and recoverable flight data.   
 
Effective implementation of ADT requires coordinated understanding between 
aircraft operators, air traffic service units (ATSU), ADT service providers, and 
rescue coordination centres (RCCs) (i.e. ARCC/ARSC).   
Note1. - ADT service, the provision of a means to make available autonomously 
transmitted position information on an aircraft in distress.

means to make available autonomously transmitted position information of an 
aircraft in distress.

Procedures for ATS Units When A Volcanic Ash Cloud Is 
Reported or Forecast 
9.1 
ATC Action 
 
If a volcanic ash cloud is reported or forecast in the airspace for which the ATSU 
is responsible, the following actions shall be taken: 
 Relay pertinent information immediately to flight crews whose aircraft could 
be affected to ensure that they are aware of the ash cloud’s current and 
forecast position and the flight levels affected; 
 Accommodate requests for re-routing or level changes to the extent 
practicable; 
 
Suggest re-routing to avoid or exit areas of reported or forecast ash clouds 
when requested by the pilot or deemed necessary by the controller; and 
 When practicable, request a special air-report when the route of flight takes 
the aircraft into or near the forecast ash cloud and provide such special air-
reports to the appropriate agencies. 
Note1. - Experience has shown that the recommended escape manoeuvre for an 
aircraft which has encountered an ash cloud is to reverse its course and begin a 
descent if terrain permits. The final responsibility for this decision, however, rests 
with the pilot-in-command as specified in the Manual on Volcanic Ash, Radioactive 
Material and Toxic Chemical Clouds (ICAO Doc 9691), Paragraph 5.2.4.1.

Wind Shear Hazards at Aerodromes 
10.1 
General 
 
Wind shear is a sustained change in wind velocity along an aircraft’s flight path, 
which occurs significantly faster than the aircraft can accelerate or decelerate. 
Wind shear can occur at any level, but it is the “low level wind shear” occurring 
from the surface to a height of approximately 1,500 ft, which causes problems of 
sufficient magnitude to affect the control of aircraft in the departure and approach 
phases of flight. 
 
At aerodromes, controllers shall be alert to the following conditions which are 
conducive to wind shear: 
 The presence of a front, squall or thunderstorm activity in the vicinity of the 
aerodrome; and 
 The presence of low-level inversion where the surface wind will be 
significantly different from that at only a few hundred feet above the ground. 
 
Controllers shall also be aware that obstructions within an aerodrome such as 
local terrain or buildings considered in relation to wind speed and direction, can 
cause wind shear in addition to the usual generation of turbulence and gusts.

serve to illustrate to controllers the hazards of low-level wind shear:

10.2 
ATC Action 
 
When a departing or arriving aircraft reports wind shear conditions to air traffic 
control, controllers shall be alert to the possibility of an abnormal landing or crash 
and, shall pass the reported wind shear to subsequent inbound and outbound 
flights until confirmation is received that the condition no longer exists. Wind shear 
reports from pilots shall contain the following information: 
 A warning of the presence of the wind shear; 
 The height or height band where the wind shear was encountered; 
 
The time at which it was encountered; and 
 Details of the effect of the wind shear on the aircraft, e.g., speed gain or loss, 
vertical speed tendency and change in drift. 
Note. - Pilots may also use the words “slight”, “moderate” or “severe” to describe 
the wind shear effect. 
 
Controllers shall use the following phraseology to transmit a wind shear condition 
to aircraft: 
“AT (time) A DEPARTING B737 REPORTED WINDSHEAR AT 300 FT. 
AIRSPEED LOSS 30 KT., STRONG LEFT DRIFT.” 
 
Controllers shall include the wind shear information in ATIS broadcasts. 
 
Controllers shall take note that pilots may delay their approach or take-off when 
wind shear conditions have been reported.

ATC Emergency Checklist 
11.1 
Introduction  
 
When an aircraft encounters an emergency or accident, the Alerting service 
provided by ATCO is crucial.  
 
Failure to take actions based on established procedures will cause delays in the 
ATS unit channelling necessary information to the relevant party/officer for 
ARCC/ARSC activation for search and rescue efforts.  
11.2 
Purpose  
 
The purpose of procedure is to provide information on the ATC Emergency 
Checklist, as a guideline for managing an emergency.  
 
The checklist in Attachment 2 - ATC Emergency Checklist, shall be placed at all 
controller working positions (CWP), for easy reference and fast actions taken by 
the ATCOs.  
 
The ATCOs must complete the information (including time check and specifics 
details) as follows: 
 Name of ATSU and ATCO;  
 Aircraft/Vehicle Information;  
 
Emergency Details and Declaration;  
 Actions by ATC; and  
 Other Actions Taken and Remarks. 
 
The completed form shall be passed to the ATCC WM for the next course of action.
