Annex A 
Action by the Recipient of a Bomb Threat Telephone Call. 
 
1. 
The following basic questions shall always be asked by the recipient of a bomb threat 
telephone call immediately the nature of the call is determined in order to assist in the 
determination of the required response actions by the appropriate authority or agency 
tasked with handling such threats: 
a) 
What time is the bomb set to explode? 
b) 
Where is the bomb placed? 
c) 
What kind of device is it? 
d) 
What does it look like? 
e) 
Why did you place the bomb? 
2. 
The recipient shall record only the exact words used by the caller in the initial 
conversation and in reply to the questions. It is important that the recipient listens 
carefully at all times and, in addition, be able to describe the caller’s voice by sex, age 
and tone, determine whether or not the voice is familiar and note any background 
noises which may assist in determining the location from which the call is being made. 
No attempt shall be made to interpret the words used by the caller. 
3. 
If it is at all possible, the recipient shall, immediately and by means of a discreet signal, 
arrange for another person to monitor the telephone conversation. That person shall 
also record the exact words used by the caller, making no attempt to interpret the 
conversion.

General 
1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 16 - Miscellaneous 
Procedures, Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 16 - Miscellaneous Procedures shall 
be read together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 2, CAD 10 Volume II, CAD 11, 
CAD 1101, CAD 15 and International Civil Aviation Organization Doc 8400. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 16 - Miscellaneous Procedures contains standard 
operating procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other 
operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their 
area of responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026. 
1.4 
Interpretation of Words 
Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil 
Aviation Authority of Malaysia Act 2017 [Act 788].  
May means the procedure/instruction is permissive, optional or alternative. 
Miles always refers to nautical miles (NM). 
Shall, is to, are to and must means the instruction is mandatory.

Responsibility in Regard to Military Traffic 
2.1 
Responsibility 
 
It is recognised that some military aeronautical operations necessitate non-
compliance with certain air traffic procedures. In order to ensure the safety of flight 
operations the appropriate military authorities shall be asked, whenever 
practicable, to notify the appropriate Air Traffic Services Unit (ATSU) prior to 
undertaking such manoeuvres. 
 
A reduction of separation minima required by military necessity or other 
extraordinary circumstances shall only be accepted by an ATSU when a specific 
request in some recorded form has been obtained from the authority having 
jurisdiction over the aircraft concerned and the lower minima then to be observed 
shall apply only between those aircraft. Some recorded form of instruction fully 
covering this reduction of separation minima must be issued by the ATSU 
concerned. 
 
Temporary airspace reservation, either stationary or mobile, may be established 
for the use of large formation flights or other military air operations. Arrangements 
for the reservation of such airspace shall be accomplished by coordination 
between the airspace users and CAAM through the Chief Executive Officer (CEO). 
The coordination shall be affected in accordance with the provisions of CAD 11

Strategic Lateral Offset Procedures 
Note1. - Strategic Lateral Offset Procedures (SLOP) are approved procedures that allow 
aircraft to fly on a parallel track to the right of the centre line relative to the direction of flight to 
mitigate the lateral overlap probability due to increased navigation accuracy and wake 
turbulence encounters. Unless specified in the separation standard, an aircraft’s use of these 
procedures does not affect the application of prescribed separation standards. 
Note2. - CAD 2, Paragraph 3.6.2.1.1, requires authorisation for the application of strategic 
lateral offsets from the appropriate ATS authority responsible for the airspace concerned. 
4.1 
Procedures 
 
Implementation of SLOP shall be coordinated among the states involved. 
Note. - Information concerning the implementation of strategic lateral offset 
procedures is contained in the Implementation of Strategic Lateral Offset 
Procedures (Circular 354). 
 
Strategic Lateral Offsets shall be authorised only in en route airspace as follows: 
 Where the lateral separation minima or spacing between route centre lines is 
15 NM (28 km) or more, offsets to the right of the centre line relative to the 
direction of flight in tenths of a nautical mile up to a maximum of 2 NM (3.7 
km); and

Prohibition of Landing on Water Catchment Areas 
5.1 
Introduction 
 
Water catchment areas are classified as national assets, and designated as 
Restricted Areas therefore, landing or low flying activity over these areas are 
strictly prohibited. CAAM had consulted the National Security Council and the 
Chief Government Security Office on restrictions over these areas and would like 
to provide some guidance to prevent similar incidents from reoccurring in future. 
5.2

Air traffic controllers are required to adhere the instructions stipulated in this 
section but it’s not limited to the following responsibilities. Air traffic controllers are 
obliged to take preventive action should there be flights that intend to operate in 
the vicinity of water catchment areas. 
5.3 
Responsibility of Air Traffic Controllers 
 
Air traffic controllers shall take note of the following items in the flight plan: 
 Aircraft type (whether it’s an amphibious aircraft); 
 Operating area/destination (whether in the vicinity of water catchment areas); 
 
If destination is in the vicinity of water catchment areas, inquire their intention; 
 If the aircraft intends to operate in the vicinity of any water catchment areas, 
request for their approval letter obtained from the relevant authorities, if

 Establish and maintain a database of RVSM approvals;

Large Height Deviation (LHD)  
 
In general, LHD means a vertical deviation of 300 FT or more from controller 
assigned or coordinated flight level, for any reason, regardless whether the 
deviation causes an incident or not.   
 
The deviation may be due to controller error, pilot error, equipment malfunction or 
other environmental factors such as turbulence, causing the aircraft to be at a 
vertical position that is unexpected by the controller.   
 
The causal errors and examples of LHD are classified in the following taxonomy, 
whereby any LHD reports to MAAR should be in accordance with the listed codes.  
 
Code  
LHD Cause  
Operational Errors  
A  
Flight crew failing to climb/descend the aircraft as cleared  
 
Example: Aircraft A was at FL300 and assigned FL360. A Cleared Level Adherence 
Monitoring (CLAM) alert was seen as the aircraft passed FL364. The Mode C level 
reached FL365 before descending back to FL360.  
 
B  
Flight crew climbing/descending without air traffic control (ATC) clearance

LHD Hot Spots  
 
In 2022, six LHD hot spots were identified in the South Asia/Indian Ocean (SA/IO) 
and Southeast Asian (SEA) airspaces. These hot spots were determined based 
on mid-air collision risk estimates from January to December of that year. 
 
4 of the hotspots involved Malaysian FIRs, and they are;  
 LHD Hot Spot A2 (Chennai and Kuala Lumpur FIRs);  
 LHD Hot Spot D (Manila and all adjacent FIRs);  
 
LHD Hot Spot J (Singapore/Kota Kinabalu-Jakarta FIRs); and  
 LHD Hot Spot O (Bangkok/Ho Chi Minh/Kuala Lumpur and Singapore FIRs).

General 
 
INMARSAT, in conjunction with ICAO, has developed a telephone numbering 
plan to facilitate the use of satellite voice by suitably equipped aircraft as a 
backup to the existing primary A/G facilities. The use of SATCOM voice for this 
purpose requires on board embedded equipment. 
 
Flight Crew Procedures 
 
The number of call attempts made to establish contact with the radio station will 
be a pilot responsibility; however, if contact cannot be established within 5 
minutes of waypoint transition, pilots should revert to the assigned HF 
frequencies for position report delivery. 
 
On initial contact with a radio station, the flight crew should provide aircraft 
identification and request frequency assignment and perform a successful 
SELCAL check on HF, when required by the CEO. Subsequent 
communications with that radio station may then be performed via SATCOM or 
HF voice, in accordance with applicable airworthiness, operating and airspace 
requirements. 
 
Although the underlying technology lends itself to a conversational mode of 
communications, such use can create misunderstanding and confusion. When 
using SATCOM, normal RTF conventions should be followed identical to HF 
communications in accordance with standard ICAO phraseology, as defined in
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 16 - MISCELLANEOUS PROCEDURES (03072026).pdf

Although the underlying technology lends itself to a conversational mode of 
communications, such use can create misunderstanding and confusion. When 
using SATCOM, normal RTF conventions should be followed identical to HF 
communications in accordance with standard ICAO phraseology, as defined in 
Jeppesen ATC- Air Traffic Management (ICAO Doc 4444) \ Section 12, or in 
Annex 10, Volume II, Chapter 5 and ICAO Doc 8400. 
 
The flight crew should normally make calls to the radio facility serving the 
airspace in which the aircraft is flying. If oceanic airspace has not been entered, 
the flight crew should attempt contact with the radio facility serving the first 
oceanic centre. If a call is dropped during a communication, the party that 
initiated the original call should initiate the process to re-establish the call. If 
communications are lost with the current aeronautical station, the flight crew 
should attempt contact with any other aeronautical station to relay. 
 
If a HF SELCAL check is required before or after entering a FIR, the flight crew 
should contact the radio operator and complete a HF SELCAL check in 
accordance with ICAO Annex 10, Volume II, paragraph 5.2.4.

Airspace Management 
2.1 
Introduction 
 
By international agreement, Malaysia is responsible for the management of the 
airspace and provision of Air Traffic Services (ATS) within the Kuala Lumpur and 
Kota Kinabalu Flight Information Regions (FIRs) and in the South China Sea 
Corridor. Through bilateral agreements, the Air Traffic Services Centres at Kuala 
Lumpur and Kota Kinabalu provide ATS in certain airspace delegated by ATS 
authorities of adjacent FIRs. 
 
The Civil Aviation Regulations 2016 and the relevant ICAO Annexes empower the 
Minister of Transport and the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of CAAM to regulate 
the conduct of air navigation in the two FIRs. Thus, the organisation of airspace 
and provision of air traffic services is in compliance with ICAO. 
 
Airspace activities within the FIRs are not only confined to commercial, private and 
military aviation activities but also include air and surface firing, military training, 
parachute jumping and other activities. 
 
Portions of the airspace in the FIRs have been delineated specifically for safety 
and national security reasons, e.g., to facilitate the provision of air traffic services 
and the conduct of military operations. Some of the activities are incompatible and, 
therefore, require segregation from each other. Certain portions of the airspace
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 17 - AIRSPACE MANAGEMENT (03072026).pdf

and national security reasons, e.g., to facilitate the provision of air traffic services 
and the conduct of military operations. Some of the activities are incompatible and, 
therefore, require segregation from each other. Certain portions of the airspace

services in this airspace has been vested with the military. 
 
While the CAAM, the administrative authority, has national responsibility for the 
management of the airspace and the provision of air traffic services in the FIRs, it 
does so on a cooperative basis with the military, which has responsibility for 
national airspace security. 
2.2 
Airspace Administration 
 
Though the primary users of the airspace are civil aircraft operators and the 
military, no single party can claim exclusivity to its use. In planning the organisation 
of the airspace, the principle that shall be adhered to is that airspace organisation 
must provide for an equitable sharing of its use by all those having a legitimate 
interest in it. The objective should be to organise the airspace so that the parties 
concerned can use it most flexibly through a coordinated effort. Furthermore, 
because of the international character of civil aviation, airspace planning of 
necessity should consider regional needs.

Airspace Classification 
3.1 
General 
 
The airspace in the two FIRs is classified in accordance with the ICAO 
classification of airspace with the exception that two-way radio communication is 
required of Visual Flight Rules (VFR) aircraft in all classes of airspace. Whenever 
a controlled area is designated, it shall be designated in accordance with this 
classification.  
 
The ATS airspace classifications are as follows: 
Class A 
Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) flights only are permitted. All flights 
are subject to air traffic control service and are separated from 
each other. 
Class B 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. All flights are subject to air 
traffic control service and are separated from each other. 
Class C 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. All flights are subject to air 
traffic control service and IFR flights are separated from other 
IFR flights and from VFR flights. VFR flights are separated from 
IFR flights and receive traffic information in respect of other VFR 
flights. 
Class D 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. All flights are subject to air 
traffic control service. IFR flights are separated from other IFR 
flights and receive traffic information in respect of VFR flights. 
VFR flights receive traffic information in respect of all other 
flights. 
Class E 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. IFR flights are provided with

flights and receive traffic information in respect of VFR flights.

air traffic control service and are separated from other IFR

Control areas including, inter alia, airways are established to encompass sufficient 
airspace to contain the flight paths of those IFR flights or portions thereof to which 
it is desired to provide the applicable parts of the air traffic control service, taking 
into account the capabilities of the navigation aids normally used in that area. 
CTAs usually consist of Terminal Control Area (TMA), Control Zone (CTR) and 
Aerodrome Traffic Zone (ATZ).

Chapter 4 - Airspace Reservations and Block Clearances 
 
 
 
 
4-1
4 
Airspace Reservations and Block Clearances 
4.1 
General 
 
Notwithstanding the designation of an airspace for a specific purpose, certain 
activities may require the temporary release of airspace by one controlling 
authority to the other for specific periods. Such release of airspace shall be 
undertaken by the airspace reservation or block clearance systems described 
herein. 
4.2 
Distinction Between the Block Clearance and Airspace Reservation Systems 
 
A block clearance is an authorisation by a controlling authority for the release of 
airspace, or a defined portion thereof, to another controlling authority for a 
significant period of time to permit aircraft to usefully utilise that airspace.  
 
Examples of circumstances that would require the issue of a block clearance are 
given below: 
 When a military-restricted area is being used by limited military aircraft, which 
will permit other aircraft operations to be confined to agreed sectors or 
geographical areas or height bands within that area; and 
 In civil control areas, civil traffic may be required to confine their operations to 
agreed flight levels or make minor diversions to permit passage of military

rescue aid, and assist such organisations as required.

Determination of The Need for Air Traffic Services 
 
The provision of air traffic services shall be determined by consideration of the 
following: 
 The types of air traffic involved; 
 The density of air traffic; 
 
The meteorological conditions; 
 Such other factors as may be relevant. 
Note. - Due to the number of elements involved, it has not been possible to 
develop specific data to determine the need for air traffic services in a given area 
or at a given location. For example: 
a) a mixture of different types of air traffic with aircraft of varying speeds 
(conventional jet, etc.) might necessitate the provision of air traffic services, 
whereas a relatively greater density of traffic where only one type of operation 
is involved would not; 
b) meteorological conditions might have considerable effect in areas where there 
is a constant flow of air traffic (e.g., scheduled traffic), whereas similar or worse 
meteorological conditions might be relatively unimportant in an area where air 
traffic would be discontinued in such conditions (e.g., local VFR flights); 
c) open stretches of water, mountainous, uninhabited or desert areas might 
necessitate the provision of air traffic services even though the frequency of 
operations is extremely low.

General 
 
The purpose of contingency plan is to provide a safe and orderly flow of domestic 
and international air traffic in the event of disruptions of air traffic services and 
related supporting services.

 Develop contingency plans for introduction in respect of generally foreseeable 
events such as industrial action or labour unrest affecting the air traffic 
services and or supporting services; and  
 Monitor any developments which might lead to events requiring contingency 
measures to be applied.

 Airspace management; 
 Traffic densities; 
 
Complexity of airspace arrangements and pilot/ATC procedures;

 Foreign state aircraft which have already been given diplomatic approval; 
 
En route international flights and 
 The alternate level of personnel, services and facilities available.

Introduction

reasonable, workplace fatigue and its risks, to ensure a safe and error-free work 
environment for employees, contractors and clients. The objectives of the Fatigue

 Controllers are fit for work; 
 The organisation enjoys a safe working environment by minimising hazards 
associated with fatigue; 
 
The fatigue hazards associated with long work hours and shift works are 
minimised; 
 All personnel have access to gain assistance through a range of preventative 
initiatives, including training; 
 Informed or joint decisions are to be made regarding work design; 
 
On-going risk assessment and hazard monitoring takes place; and

and fairly.

5.1 
Prior Sleep Opportunity 
 
When controller rostered for duty, he must have at least enough rest so that he is 
fit for the commencement of his duty. Unless a unique arrangement has been 
agreed to between the controller and ATSU Director/ATS Airport Manager (or 
delegated person) and recorded. 
5.2 
Minimum Rest Period 
 
Sleep deprivation, leading to the onset of fatigue, can arise if an air traffic controller 
is required to report early for duty on a number of consecutive days. Therefore, 
not more than 3 consecutive duties that occur in any part of the night period 0001 
to 0600 hours local time can be undertaken and not more than 6 consecutive days 
of duties shall be rostered.   
 
However, air traffic controller who is employed on a regular night duty for a 
maximum of 3 consecutive duties shall work to the following: 
 The minimum rest period before the start of such duties is 12 hours; 
 The duty shall not exceed 10 hours; 
 
At the finish of such a series of duties, controller shall have a minimum of 54 
hours free from all duties. 
 
While air traffic controller who is employed on a regular duty for 6 consecutive 
days of duties, shall work to following: 
 The minimum rest period before the start of such duties is 12 hours; 
 The duty shall not exceed 12 hours;

5.4 
Commuting Time 
a) Commute time, other than that time spent on duty positioning, does not count as 
duty; 
b) Travelling time, from home to workstation, if long distances are involved, is a 
factor influencing any subsequent onset of fatigue. If the journey time from home 
to normal workstation is usually more than 30 km, air traffic controller shall make 
arrangements for temporary accommodation nearer to workstation. 
5.5 
Delayed in A Single Duty 
 
When air traffic controller is known of a delay to the reporting duty time before 
leaving the place of rest, the duty shall be calculated as follows.  
 When the delay is less than 2 hours, the maximum duty period allowed will be 
based on the original report time and the duty will start at the actual report 
time.  
 When the delay is more than 2 hours, the maximum duty period will be 
calculated using the more limiting of the planned and actual report times and 
the duty will start 2 hours after the original report time. 
5.6 
Access to Sustenance 
 
In order to avoid any detriment to an air traffic controller’s performance, 
opportunities to consume a meal must be arranged when the duty period exceeds 
6 hours. 
 
A pantry complete with food and beverages storage and food heating and cooling 
appliances shall be provided to facilitate access to adequate sustenance.

Extensions 
 
Duty time extension shall only be authorised in unforeseen operational 
circumstances where other possible solutions to operational issues are 
unavailable.  
 
Director shall authorise an extension to a duty time limit. To do so, the Director 
shall consider the increased operational risks including: 
 Impacts from increased workloads; 
 Impact on the controller’s duty expectations; 
 
Environmental factors including weather and temperature;  
 Availability of assigning alternate controller; 
 Possibility of reducing traffic capacity; 
 
Future rostering or planning implications of the extension; and 
 Opportunities for duty rest. 
 
Duty shall only be extended if: 
 The controllers consider themselves fit for the extended duty. They should 
undertake an alertness consideration review and agree to the extension via 
the communication protocol; 
 The controllers have had sufficient time to consider their fatigue levels and 
agree to the extension; 
 
The duty is extended by no more than 2 hours; 
 Cumulative flight or duty limits are not exceeded.

Introduction 
 
This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that 
provides guidance and standards for the provision of air traffic services. The ANSM is ANSD 
internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1. 
The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective. 
Throughout this MATS Volume 1, the use of masculine pronouns should be understood to 
represent male and female persons.

General 
1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 19 - Search and Rescue 
(SAR), Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this, MATS Volume 1 Part 19 - Search and Rescue (SAR) shall 
be read together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 11, CAD 1101, CAD 12, 
International Civil Aviation Organization Doc 9731 and ANSM 5 - Aeronautical 
Search and Rescue Manual. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1 Part 19 - Search and Rescue (SAR) contains standard 
operating procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other 
operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their 
area of responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026. 
1.4 
Interpretation of Words 
Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil 
Aviation Authority of Malaysia Act 2017 [Act 788]. 
May means the procedure/instruction is permissive, optional or alternative. 
Miles always refers to nautical miles (NM). 
Shall, is to, are to and must means the instruction is mandatory.

2.1 
Introduction 
 
Aeronautical Search and Rescue (SAR) is broadly defined as the search for 
aircraft in distress (or referred to as an “aeronautical incident”) and the provision 
of aid to persons who are, or feared to be, in need of assistance, regardless of the 
nationality or status of such persons or the circumstances in which such persons 
are found, whether it occurs over land or sea. 
 
Aeronautical SAR services in Malaysia are provided by the Civil Aviation Authority 
of Malaysia (CAAM), as the Lead SAR Authority in collaboration with the 
Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA), Royal Military Air Force 
(RMAF), Royal Malaysian Navy (RMN), Royal Malaysia Police (RMP), Marine 
Department and Fire and Rescue Department Malaysia. 
 
The services are available on a 24-hour basis by the provisions stipulated in CAD 
12 - Search and Rescue. The International Aeronautical and Maritime SAR 
Manual (IAMSAR Manual) ICAO Doc 9731: Vol. I, II and III are the reference 
documents for the international requirements.

2.2 
CAAM SAR and Disaster Management Objective 
Note. - See ANSM 5 – ASARM, Chapter 3, Para 3.1. for CAAM SAR and Disaster 
Management Objective. 
 
CAAM’s objectives for SAR and Disaster Management within Malaysia are as 
follows:  
 Support the National SAR Committee's objectives and implement Malaysia's 
Aeronautical SAR Policy issued by the National Security Council through 2 
core activities: SAR Operations and Prevention; 
 Determine Malaysia's Aeronautical SAR policies and practices in line with 
International Civil Aviation Organisation and International requirement; 
 
Provide and coordinate SAR services for aircraft in distress within the Kuala 
Lumpur and Kota Kinabalu Search and Rescue Regions (SRRs) and in other 
areas as permitted by the Minister; and 
 When applicable, support and assist disaster management activities and 
operations at District, State, and National levels.

Search and Rescue Procedures 
3.1 
Declaration of Emergency Phase and Notification to ARCC/ARSC 
 
The initial declaration of an emergency phase shall be the responsibility of the 
controlling agency, i.e., the ATCC or the concerned ATS unit.  
 
Controllers shall declare the appropriate emergency phase upon becoming aware 
of any emergency situation. They shall notify the ATCC WM, who would then 
activate the ARCC/ARSC. The SAR Officer, as the SMC, may declare the 
subsequent SAR phases, as required, based on their evaluation of the situation. 
Note. - See ANSM 5 – ASARM, Chapter 4, Para 4.3 for details of emergency 
phases. 
 
ARCC/ARSC shall take over the responsibility for all subsequent actions utilising 
RCC procedures. 
 
The SAR phase shall be cancelled by ARCC/ARSC, and all concerned shall be 
notified; when the aircraft has landed or resumed normal operations.

 “Activated” means ARCC/ARSC is conducting/assisting in a SAR operation.

Aeronautical SAR mission when:

reasonable hope of rescuing survivors has passed.

Cospas-Sarsat Alert Massages Handling Flow 
 
Cospas-Sarsat is best known as the system that detects and locates 
emergency beacons (operation on 406MHz), such as:   
 Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT). Used in aircraft. Activate on impact 
or by manual activation by the flight crew; 
 Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon. Used aboard the marine 
vessel; 
 
Personal Locator Beacon. Carried by the individual; 
 ELT Distress Tracking. Used in aircraft. For autonomous tracking of aircraft 
in distress. Will activate autonomously when aircraft enters threatening 
flight configurations and send these distress alerts (SIT185) to ATSU/SAR 
authorities. 
 
See the flowchart of the Cospas-Sarsat alert messages process and 
management utilising SAROCS.

Introduction 
 
This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that 
provides guidance and standards for the provision of air traffic services. The ANSM is ANSD 
internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1. 
The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective. 
Throughout this MATS Volume 1, the use of masculine pronouns should be understood to 
represent male and female persons.

1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 2 - ATS Safety 
Management, Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 2 - ATS Safety Management shall be 
read together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 11, CAD 1101, International Civil 
Aviation Organization (ICAO) Doc 7030, ICAO Doc 9426, ICAO Doc 9574, ICAO 
Doc 9613, ICAO Doc 9689 and ICAO Doc 9859. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 2 - ATS Safety Management contains standard 
operating procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other 
operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their 
area of responsibility.  
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026.

Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil 
Aviation Authority of Malaysia Act 2017 [Act 788].

Miles always refers to nautical miles (NM). 
Shall, is to, are to and must means the instruction is mandatory.

Chapter 2 - Overview

Overview 
2.1 
General 
 
ATS units (ATSUs) shall ensure that the level of Air Traffic Services (ATS) and 
Communication, Navigation and Surveillance (CNS), as well as the ATS 
procedures applicable to the airspace or aerodrome concerned, are appropriate 
and adequate for maintaining an acceptable level of safety in the provision of ATS. 
 
The requirements in respect of services, systems and procedures applicable to 
airspaces and aerodromes should be established on the basis of a regional air 
navigation agreement in order to facilitate the harmonisation of ATS in adjacent 
airspaces. 
 
To ensure that safety in the provision of ATS is maintained, the Air Navigation 
Services Divisions (ANSD) shall implement Safety Management System (SMS) 
for the ATS under its jurisdiction. Where appropriate, ATS SMS should be 
established on the basis of a regional air navigation agreement. 
 
All ATSUs shall have in place a SMS acceptable to the Secretary General (Sec-
Gen) of the Ministry of Transport (MOT), which addresses high-level safety 
objectives as follows: 
a) Identify safety hazards; 
b) Safety risk management; 
c) Ensure the implementation of remedial action necessary to maintain agreed 
safety performance; 
d) Provide for continuous monitoring and regular assessment of the safety 
performance; and 
e) Aim at continuous improvement of the overall performance of the SMS.

ATS Safety Management Activities 
4.1 
General 
 
An ATS SMS should include, inter alia, the following with respect to the provision 
of ATS: 
 Monitoring of overall safety levels and detection of any adverse trend; 
 Safety reviews of ATSU; 
 
Safety assessments in respect of the planned implementation of airspace 
reorganisations, the introduction of new equipment systems or facilities, and 
new or changed ATS procedures; and 
 A mechanism for identifying the need for safety enhancing measures. 
 
All activities undertaken in an ATS SMS shall be fully documented. All 
documentation shall be retained for such period of time as is specified by the Chief 
Executive Officer (CEO). 
Note1. - See ANSM 4 - SMM for detailed ATS safety management activities. 
Note2. - See each ATSU SMM for detailed information.

5.1 
Collection and Evaluation of Safety-Related Data 
 
Data for use in safety monitoring programmes should be collected from as wide a 
range of sources as possible, as the safety-related consequences of particular 
procedures or systems may not be realised until after an incident has occurred. 
 
ANSD should establish a formal incident reporting system for ATS personnel to 
facilitate the collection of information on actual or potential safety hazards or 
deficiencies related to the provision of ATS, including route structures, procedures, 
CNS systems and other safety significant systems and equipment as well as 
controller workloads. 
Note. - Guidance related to both mandatory and voluntary State incident reporting 
systems is contained in the Safety Management Manual (ICAO Doc 9859) and 
CAD 1900.

incident reports, shall be systematically reviewed by ANSD in order to detect any

Chapter 7 - Safety Assessments

Safety Assessments 
7.1 
Need for Safety Assessments 
 
A safety assessment shall be carried out in respect of proposals for significant 
airspace reorganisations, for significant changes in the provision of ATS 
procedures applicable to an airspace or an aerodrome, and for the introduction of 
new equipment, systems or facilities, such as: 
 A reduced separation minimum to be applied within an airspace or at an 
aerodrome; 
 A new operating procedure, including departure and arrival procedures, to be 
applied within an airspace or at an aerodrome; 
 
A reorganisation of the ATS route structure; 
 A resectorisation of an airspace; 
 Physical changes to the layout of runways and/or taxiways at an aerodrome; 
and 
 
Implementation of new communications, surveillance or other safety-
significant systems and equipment, including those providing new 
functionality and/or capabilities.

separation minimum, including a minimum based on required navigation 
performance, a reduced vertical separation minimum of 300 m (1,000 ft) between 
FL 290 and FL 410 inclusive (reduced vertical separation minimum), the reduction 
of a separation minimum based on the use of an ATS surveillance system or a 
wake turbulence separation minimum or reduction of minima between landing 
and/or departing aircraft.

Chapter 8 - Safety-Enhancing Measures

8 
Safety-Enhancing Measures 
8.1 
General 
 
Any actual or potential hazard related to the provision of ATS within an airspace 
or at an aerodrome, whether identified through an ATS safety management activity 
or by any other means, shall be assessed and classified by ANSD for its risk 
acceptability. 
 
Except when the risk can be classified as acceptable, ANSD shall, as a matter of 
priority and as far as practicable, implement appropriate measures to eliminate the 
risk or reduce the risk to a level that is acceptable. 
 
If it becomes apparent that the level of safety applicable to an airspace or an 
aerodrome is not, or may not be achieved, ANSD shall, as a matter of priority and 
as far as practicable, implement appropriate remedial measures. 
 
Implementation of any remedial measure shall be followed by an evaluation of the 
effectiveness of the measure in eliminating or mitigating a risk.

Capacity Management  
2.1 
General  
 
The capacity of an Air Traffic Services (ATS) system depends on many factors, 
including the ATS route structure, the navigation accuracy of the aircraft using the 
airspace, weather-related factors, and controller workload. Every effort should be 
made to provide sufficient capacity to cater to both normal and peak traffic levels; 
however, in implementing any measures to increase capacity, Air Navigation 
Services Divisions (ANSD) shall ensure, in accordance with the procedures 
specified relating safety levels are not jeopardised.  
 
The number of aircraft provided with an Air Traffic Control (ATC) service shall not 
exceed that which can be safely handled by the ATC unit concerned under the 
prevailing circumstances. In order to define the maximum number of flights which 
can be safely accommodated, ANSD should assess and declare the ATC capacity 
for control areas, for control sectors within a control area and for aerodromes.  
 
ATC capacity should be expressed as the maximum number of aircraft which can 
be accepted over a given period of time within the airspace or at the aerodrome 
concerned.  
Note. - The most appropriate measure of capacity is likely to be the sustainable 
hourly traffic flow. Such hourly capacities can, for example, be converted into daily, 
monthly or annual values. 
2.2 
Capacity Assessment

2.2 
Capacity Assessment  
 
In assessing capacity values, factors to be taken into account should include, inter 
alia:  
 The level and type of ATS provided;  
 The structural complexity of the control area, the control sector or the 
aerodrome concerned;  
 
Controller workload, including control and coordination tasks to be performed;  
 The types of communications, navigation and surveillance systems in use, 
their degree of technical reliability and availability as well as the availability of 
backup systems and/or procedures;  
 Availability of ATC systems providing controller support and alert functions; 
and  
 
Any other factor or element deemed relevant to controller workload.  
Note. - Summaries of techniques which may be used to estimate control 
sector/position capacities are contained in the Air Traffic Services Planning 
Manual (ICAO Doc 9426).

Regulation of ATC Capacity and Traffic Volumes  
 
Where traffic demand varies significantly on a daily or periodic basis, facilities and 
procedures should be implemented to vary the number of operational sectors or 
working positions to meet the prevailing and anticipated demand. Applicable 
procedures should be contained in local instructions.  
 
In case of particular events which have a negative impact on the declared capacity 
of an airspace or aerodrome, the capacity of the airspace or aerodrome concerned 
shall be reduced accordingly for the required time period. Whenever possible, the 
capacity pertaining to such events should be predetermined.  
 
To ensure that safety is not compromised whenever the traffic demand in an 
airspace or at an aerodrome is forecast to exceed the available ATC capacity, 
measures shall be implemented to regulate traffic volumes accordingly.

continuing and frequent traffic delays, or it becomes apparent that forecast traffic 
demand will exceed capacity values, the ANSD should, as far as practicable:

Chapter 3 - Air Traffic Flow Management 
 
 
 
3-1 
3 
Air Traffic Flow Management 
3.1 
General  
 
Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) service shall be implemented for airspace 
where traffic demand at times exceeds the defined ATC capacity.  
 
ATFM should be implemented on the basis of a regional air navigation agreement 
or, when appropriate, as a multilateral agreement.  
 
The ATFM service within a region or other defined area, should be developed and 
implemented as a centralised ATFM organisation, supported by flow management 
positions established at each Area Control Centre (ACC) within the region or area 
of applicability.  
 
Certain flights may be exempt from ATFM measures, or be given priority over other 
flights.  
 
Detailed procedures governing the provision of the ATFM measures, and service 
within a region or area should be prescribed in a regional ATFM manual or 
handbook. 
3.2 
Flow Management Procedures  
 
ATFM should be carried out in three phases:  
 Strategic planning, if the action is carried out more than one day before the 
day on which it will take effect. Strategic planning is normally carried out well 
in advance, typically two to six months ahead;  
 Pre-tactical planning, if the action is to be taken on the day before the day on 
which it will take effect; and 
 
Tactical operations, if the action is taken on the day on which it will take effect.  
3.3 
Strategic Planning

 Pre-tactical planning, if the action is to be taken on the day before the day on 
which it will take effect; and 
 
Tactical operations, if the action is taken on the day on which it will take effect.  
3.3 
Strategic Planning  
 
Strategic planning should be carried out in conjunction with ATC and the aircraft 
operators. It should consist of examining the demand for the forthcoming season, 
assessing where and when demand is likely to exceed the available ATC capacity 
and taking steps to resolve the imbalance by:  
 Arranging with the ATC authority to provide adequate capacity at the required 
place and time;  
 Rerouting certain traffic flows (traffic orientation);  
 
Scheduling or rescheduling flights as appropriate; and  
 Identifying the need for tactical ATFM measures.

Where a Traffic Orientation Scheme (TOS) is to be introduced, the routes should, 
as far as practicable, minimise the time and distance penalties for the flights 
concerned, and allow some degree of flexibility in the choice of routes, particularly 
for long-range flights.  
 
When a TOS has been agreed, details should be published by all States 
concerned in a common format.  
3.4 
Pre-Tactical Planning  
 
Pre-tactical planning should entail fine-tuning of the strategic plan in the light of 
updated demand data. During this phase:  
 Certain traffic flows may be re-routed;  
 Off-load routes may be coordinated;  
 
Tactical measures will be decided upon; and  
 Details for the ATFM plan for the following day should be published and made 
available to all concerned.  
3.5 
Tactical Operations  
 
Tactical ATFM operations should consist of:  
 Executing the agreed tactical measures in order to provide a reduced and 
even flow of traffic where demand would otherwise have exceeded capacity;  
 Monitoring the evolution of the air traffic situation to ensure that the ATFM 
measures applied are having the desired effect and to take or initiate remedial 
action when long delays are reported, including rerouting of traffic and flight 
level allocation, in order to utilise the available ATC capacity to the maximum 
extent.

Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil

May means the procedure/instruction is permissive, optional or alternative.

Shall, is to, are to and must means the instruction is mandatory.

the more definitive “shall” is unreasonable but nevertheless the controller would have 
to have a good reason for not doing so. 
Will used for informative or descriptive writing, e.g., “the pilot will…” is not an 
instruction to the controller.

separate unit.

ACC, or by a control sector within an ACC.

Aerodrome control service shall be provided by an aerodrome control tower.

separate unit.

Scope and Purpose  
 
Clearances are issued solely for expediting and separating air traffic and are 
based on known traffic conditions which affect safety in aircraft operation. Such 
traffic conditions include not only aircraft in the air and on the manoeuvring area

obstructions not permanently installed on the manoeuvring area in use.  
 
If an ATC clearance is not suitable for the pilot-in-command of an aircraft, the flight 
crew may request and, if practicable, obtain an amended clearance.

proceed only in so far as known air traffic is concerned. ATC clearances do not 
constitute authority to violate any applicable regulations for promoting the safety 
of flight operations or for any other purpose; neither do clearances relieve a pilot-
in-command of any responsibility whatsoever in connection with a possible 
violation of applicable rules and regulations.  
 
ATSUs shall issue such ATC clearances as are necessary to prevent collisions 
and to expedite and maintain an orderly flow of air traffic.  
 
ATC clearances must be issued early enough to ensure that they are transmitted

Chapter 9 - Change from IFR to VFR Flight 
 
 
 
9-1
9 
Change from IFR to VFR Flight  
9.1 
General 
 
Change from IFR flight to VFR flight is only acceptable when a message initiated 
by the pilot-in-command containing the specific expression “CANCELLING MY 
IFR FLIGHT”, together with the changes, if any, to be made to the current flight 
plan, is received by an ATSU. Controllers are not allowed to suggest or imply that a 
pilot should switch from an IFR flight to a VFR flight be it directly or by inference. 
 
No reply, other than the acknowledgment “IFR FLIGHT CANCELLED AT ... 
(time)”, should normally be made by an ATSU.  
 
When an ATSU is in possession of information that instrument meteorological 
conditions are likely to be encountered along the route of flight, a pilot changing 
from IFR flight to VFR flight should, if practicable, be so advised.  
 
Information to a pilot changing from IFR flight to VFR flight where it is likely that 
flight in VMC cannot be maintained shall be given in the following manner:  
“INSTRUMENT METEOROLOGICAL CONDITIONS REPORTED (or forecast) IN 
THE VICINITY OF (location)”.  
 
An ATSU receiving notification of an aircraft’s intention to change from IFR to VFR 
flight shall, as soon as practicable thereafter, so inform all other ATSUs to whom 
the IFR flight plan was addressed, except those units through whose regions or 
areas the flight has already passed.

Wake Turbulence  
Note. - The term “wake turbulence” is used in this context to describe the effect of the rotating 
air masses generated behind the wing tips of aircraft, in preference to the term “wake vortex” 
which describes the nature of the air masses. Detailed characteristics of wake vortices and 
their effect on aircraft are contained in the Air Traffic Services Planning Manual (ICAO Doc 
9426), Part II, Section 5.  
10.1

Except as provided for in paragraph 10.1.2, wake turbulence separation minima 
shall be based on a grouping of aircraft types into four categories according to the 
maximum certificated take-off mass as follows:  
 
SUPER (J) 
Aircraft types specified as such in ICAO Doc 8643, Aircraft 
Type Designators; 
HEAVY (H) 
Aircraft types of 136 000 kg or more, with the exception of 
aircraft types listed in Doc 8643 in the SUPER (J) category; 
MEDIUM (M) 
Aircraft types less than 136 000 kg but more than 7 000 kg; 
LIGHT (L) 
Aircraft types of 7 000 kg or less. 
Note. - The wake turbulence category for each aircraft type is contained in ICAO 
Doc 8643, Aircraft Type Designators.

utilising wake turbulence groups and shall be based on wake generation and

11.1 
General  
 
Altimeter setting procedures by pilots is specified in the AIP Malaysia. The unit 
used to express altimeter settings is hectopascals (hPA) and is normally rounded 
down to the nearest whole unit. Aerodrome pressure settings may be given to the 
nearest tenth of a unit if requested by the pilot. Additionally, pressure settings may 
be given in inches when requested by pilots.  
 
Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei have agreed to establish a common transition 
altitude of 11,000 ft and a transition level of FL 130 in the Kuala Lumpur, Kota 
Kinabalu and Singapore FIRs. The exception is an area formed by a radius 10 NM 
centred on Mount Kinabalu where the lowest safe altitude is 15,000 ft and the 
lowest safe level is FL 170. This arrangement has been possible because the QNH 
values in these FIRs do not vary by more than 10 hPA either side of the standard 
1013.2 setting thus ensuring at least 1,000 ft vertical separation between 11,000 
ft and FL 130 or, in the Mount Kinabalu area, between 15,000 ft and FL 170.

Area QNH  
 
The Area QNH is the forecast value of the lowest mean sea level pressure within

any location within the Area QNH Zone during the period of its validity.  
 
The Area QNH will be issued by the Meteorological Services and controllers shall 
pass this information to pilots as appropriate. An update will be issued whenever 
the mean sea level pressure at any location in the Area QNH Zone is forecast to 
fall below the current Area QNH by more than two hPA.

Determination of the Transition Level  
 
The appropriate ATSU shall establish the transition level to be used in the vicinity 
of the aerodrome(s) concerned and, when relevant, the TMA concerned, for the 
appropriate period of time on the basis of QNH (altimeter subscale setting to obtain 
elevation when on the ground) reports and forecast mean sea level pressure, if 
required.

 Area QNH - Outside TMAs, CTRs and Aerodrome Traffic Zones.

transition altitude established for the aerodrome(s) concerned. Where a common 
transition altitude has been established for two or more aerodromes which are so 
closely located as to require coordinated procedures, the appropriate ATSUs shall 
establish a common transition level to be used at any given time in the vicinity of 
the aerodrome and, when relevant, in the TMA concerned.  
 
The change from the Aerodrome/Area QNH to the standard pressure setting and 
vice versa will be affected by pilots as follows:  
 Climbing:  from QNH to the standard setting on passing the Transition Altitude.  
 Descending:  from standard setting to QNH on passing the Transition Level.  
Note. - See para 11.5.2 regarding the determination of the lowest usable flight 
level(s) for CTAs.

Position Reporting  
12.1 
Transmission of Position Reports  
 
On routes defined by designated significant points, position reports shall be made 
by the aircraft when over, or as soon as possible after passing, each designated 
compulsory reporting point, except as provided in paragraph 12.1.3 and paragraph 
12.3. Additional reports over other points may be requested by the appropriate 
ATSU.  
 
On routes not defined by designated significant points, position reports shall be 
made by the aircraft as soon as possible after the first half hour of flight and at 
hourly intervals thereafter, except as provided in paragraph 12.1.3. Additional 
reports at shorter intervals of time may be requested by the appropriate ATSU.  
 
Under conditions specified by the CEO flights may be exempted from the 
requirement to make position reports at each designated compulsory reporting 
point or interval. In applying this, account should be taken of the meteorological 
requirement for the making and reporting of routine aircraft observations.  
Note. - This is intended to apply in cases where adequate flight progress data are 
available from other sources, e.g., radar or Automatic Dependent Surveillance - 
Broadcast (ADS-B) (see Part 8), or ADS-C (see Part 13) and in other 
circumstances where the omission of routine reports from selected flights is found 
to be acceptable.

5. MONITORING FLIGHT MOVEMENTS 
 
ATCOs play a critical role in monitoring and managing flight movements from the moment a 
flight plan is filed, through all phases of the flight, including departure and arrival. The process 
begins with filing a flight plan, which contains key details such as the intended route, altitude, 
and estimated time of departure. Once the flight plan is filed, ATCOs ensures that the flight is 
scheduled and that any delays are communicated appropriately to avoid congestion in 
airspace or at airports. 
 
Upon departure, a DEP message is generated and sent by ATCOs to indicate that the aircraft 
has taken off. This message confirms that the flight has commenced and updates relevant 
stakeholders about the aircraft’s status. ATCOs continue to monitor the aircraft's progress 
throughout the flight, providing instructions and updates as necessary. 
 
Finally, upon arrival, an ARR message is created to indicate that the flight has landed 
successfully. This message marks the completion of the flight and updates the system to 
reflect that the aircraft has arrived at its destination. Throughout this process, ATCOs ensure 
that all phases of flight are coordinated smoothly, promoting safe and efficient air traffic 
management.

1. From the left-hand menu, click Outbound Flights.

This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that

internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1.

the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective.

The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 6 - Separation in the

The MATS Volume 1, Part 6 - Separation in the Vicinity of Aerodromes contains 
standard operating procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers 
and other operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services 
under their area of responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller.

This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026.

Reduction in Separation Minima in the Vicinity of Aerodromes 
2.1 
Introduction 
 
In addition to the circumstances mentioned in Part 5, Chapter 12 - Reduction in 
Separation Minima, the separation minima detailed in Part 5, Chapter 5.1 - Lateral 
Separation and Chapter 5.2 - Longitudinal Separation, may be reduced in the 
vicinity of aerodromes if: 
 Adequate separation can be provided by the aerodrome controller when each 
aircraft is continuously visible to the controller; or  
 Each aircraft is continuously visible to flight crews of the other aircraft 
concerned and the pilots thereof report that they can maintain their own 
separation; or  
 
In the case of one aircraft following another, the flight crew of the succeeding 
aircraft reports that the other aircraft is in sight and separation can be 
maintained.

General  
 
Information on essential local traffic known to the controller shall be transmitted 
without delay to departing and arriving aircraft concerned.

personnel on or near the runway to be used, or traffic in the take-off and climb-out 
area or the final approach area, which may constitute a collision hazard to a 
departing or arriving aircraft.  
Note2. - See also Part 5, Chapter 11 - Essential Traffic Information, Part 7, 
paragraph 5.3 - Essential Local Traffic Information and Part 8, paragraph 9.2 - 
Collision Hazard Information.

concern.

Procedures for Departing Aircraft 
4.1 
General 
 
Clearance for departing aircraft shall specify, when necessary for the separation 
of aircraft, direction of take-off and turn after take-off: heading or track to be made 
good before taking up the cleared departure track; level to maintain before 
continuing climb to assigned level; time, point and/or rate at which a level change 
shall be made; and any other necessary manoeuvre consistent with safe operation 
of the aircraft. 
 
At aerodromes where, Standard Instrument Departures (SIDs) have been 
established, departing aircraft should normally be cleared to follow the appropriate 
SID. 
 
The Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) service within a region or other defined 
area, should be developed and implemented as a centralised ATFM organisation, 
supported by flow management positions established at each Area Control Centre 
(ACC) within the region or area of applicability.  
 
Certain flights may be exempt from ATFM measures, or be given priority over other 
flights.  
 
Detailed procedures governing the provision of the ATFM measures, and service 
within a region or area should be prescribed in a regional ATFM manual or 
handbook.

The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) should, wherever possible, establish 
standardised procedures for the transfer of control between the Air Traffic 
Services Units (ATSUs) concerned and standard clearances for departing 
aircraft. 
Note. - The provisions applying to standardised procedures for coordination

 Where standard clearances for departing aircraft have been agreed to between 
the units concerned, the aerodrome control tower will normally issue the 
appropriate standard clearance without prior coordination with or approval from 
the approach control unit or ACC. 
 
Prior coordination of clearances should be required only in the event that a 
variation to the standard clearance or the standardised transfer of control 
procedures is necessary or desirable for operational reasons.

This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe

internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1.

the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective.

context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller.

Functions of Aerodrome Control Towers 
2.1 
General 
 
Aerodrome control towers shall issue information and clearances to aircraft under 
their control to achieve a safe, orderly and expeditious flow of air traffic on and in 
the vicinity of an aerodrome with the object of preventing collision(s) between: 
 Aircraft flying within the designated area of responsibility of the control tower, 
including the aerodrome traffic circuits;  
 Aircraft operating on the manoeuvring area;  
 
Aircraft landing and taking off;  
 Aircraft and vehicles operating on the manoeuvring area; and 
 Aircraft on the manoeuvring area and obstructions on that area. 
 
Aerodrome controllers shall maintain a continuous watch on all flight operations 
on and in the vicinity of an aerodrome as well as vehicles and personnel on the 
manoeuvring area. Watch shall be maintained by visual observation, augmented 
when available by an Air Traffic Services (ATS) surveillance system. Traffic shall 
be controlled in accordance with the procedures set forth herein and all applicable 
traffic rules specified by the Chief Executive Officer (CEO). If there are other 
aerodromes within a control zone, traffic at all aerodromes within such a zone shall 
be coordinated so that traffic circuits do not conflict. 
Note. - Provisions for the use of an ATS surveillance system in the aerodrome
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 7 - PROCEDURES FOR AERODROME CONTROL SERVICE (03072026).pdf

text:
aerodromes within a control zone, traffic at all aerodromes within such a zone shall 
be coordinated so that traffic circuits do not conflict. 
Note. - Provisions for the use of an ATS surveillance system in the aerodrome 
control service are contained in Part 8, Chapter 11 - Use of ATS Surveillance 
Systems in the Aerodrome Control Service. 
 
Visual observation shall be achieved through direct out-of-the-window 
observation, or through indirect observation utilising a visual surveillance system 
which is specifically approved for the purpose by the appropriate Air Traffic 
Services Unit (ATSU). 
 
Automatic Recording of Surveillance Data 
 
Surveillance data from primary and secondary radar equipment or other 
systems [e.g., Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast (ADS-B), 
Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Contract (ADS-C)], used as an aid to air 
traffic services, shall be automatically recorded for use in accident and incident 
investigations, search and rescue, Air Traffic Control (ATC) and surveillance 
systems evaluation and training. 
 
Automatic recordings shall be retained for a period of at least 30 days. When 
the recordings are pertinent to accident and incident investigations, they shall 
be retained for longer periods until it is evident that they will no longer be 
required.

General 
 
The term “runway-in-use” shall be used to indicate the runway or runways that, at 
a particular time, are considered by the aerodrome control tower to be the most 
suitable for use by the types of aircraft expected to land or take-off at the 
aerodrome.  
Note. - Separate or multiple runways may be designated runway-in-use for arriving 
aircraft and departing aircraft. 
 
Normally, an aircraft will land and take-off into wind unless factors such as safety, 
the runway configuration, meteorological conditions and available instrument 
approach procedures or air-traffic condition determines that a different direction is 
preferable.

and the approach and landing aids available. Runway change shall only take place 
after coordination with approach the suitable time in conjunction with traffic 
position.

Start-Up Time Procedures 
Note. - Part 11, paragraph 2.4 regarding flight information messages.  
 
When so requested by the pilot prior to engine start, an expected take-off time 
should be given, unless engine start-up time procedures are employed. 
 
Start-up time procedures should be implemented where necessary to avoid 
congestion and excessive delays on the manoeuvring area or when warranted by 
Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) regulations. Start-up time procedures should 
be contained in local instructions, and should specify the criteria and conditions 
for determining when and how start-up times shall be calculated and issued to 
departing flights.

accordance with its allocated slot time.

specified by the CEO, an aircraft should be cleared to start up at its own discretion.

specified by the CEO, the aerodrome control tower should issue an expected start-

In the event the aerodrome controller, after a take-off clearance or a landing

 Cancel the take-off clearance for a departing aircraft;

aircraft to taxi on the surface, the following provisions are applicable.

heavier helicopters.

Introduction 
 
Aerodromes taxiway stop bars are used to protect taxiway routes and runways 
from inadvertent incursions.

off to indicate that traffic may proceed.

by ATS.

clearance to proceed, the stop bar is turned off and the lead-on lights are turned 
on.

when it is intended that the runway will be used in runway visual range 
conditions less than a value of 350 m, except where:

 Aircraft on the manoeuvring area to one at a time; and 
 Vehicles on the manoeuvring area to the essential minimum. 
 
Aerodrome Operator should withdraw inoperable or non-compliance taxiway 
stop-bars from service.

latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective.

Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 9 - Flight Information 
Service and Alerting Service, Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 
July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 9 - Flight Information Service and 
Alerting Service shall be read together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 11, CAD 
1101, International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Doc 9683, ICAO Doc 9869 
and ICAO Doc 10037. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 9 - Flight Information Service and Alerting Service 
contains standard operating procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic 
controllers and other operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic 
services under their area of responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3

This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026.

Flight Information Service (FIS) shall be provided to all aircraft which are likely to 
be affected by the information and which are: 
 Provided with air traffic control service; or 
 Otherwise known to the relevant Air Traffic Services Units (ATSUs). 
Note. - FIS does not relieve the pilot-in-command of an aircraft of any 
responsibilities and the pilot-in-command has to make the final decision regarding 
any suggested alteration of flight plan.

of air traffic control service shall have precedence over the provision of flight 
information service whenever the provision of air traffic control service so requires. 
Note. - It is recognised that in certain circumstances aircraft on final approach, 
landing, take-off and climb may require to receive without delay essential 
information other than that pertaining to the provision of air traffic control service.

Executive Summary 
The National Aviation Navigation Plan (NANP) is Malaysia’s comprehensive master planning 
document, outlining the strategic direction for the safe, efficient, cost-effective, and 
environmentally sustainable management of air navigation services. Its core objective is to 
guide the industry in thorough planning and implementation initiatives, ensuring the future 
development and delivery of efficient and effective Air Navigation Services. 
 
The NANP delineates Malaysia’s planning framework to synchronise with both Regional and 
Global objectives, fostering a high degree of harmonisation and interoperability with other 
States. It also establishes the responsibilities for providing safe and efficient air navigation 
services within Malaysian airspace and for upgrading and modernizing communication, 
navigation, and surveillance facilities and services. 
 
In alignment with international efforts under the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) 
Global Air Navigation Plan (GANP), ICAO Aviation System Block Upgrade (ASBU) and the

Introduction 
 
ICAO Global Air Navigation Plan (GANP) 
 
The ICAO Global Air Navigation Plan (GANP) is designed to guide complementary 
and sector wide air transport progress over 2016–2030 and represents a rolling, 
15-year strategic methodology which leverages existing technologies and 
anticipates future developments based on State/ industry agreed operational 
objectives in addressing growth and realizing the promise of twenty-first century 
air traffic management (ATM) through a harmonised global air navigation system. 
 
The objective of ICAO GANP is to increase capacity and improve the efficiency of 
the global civil aviation system whilst improving and maintaining safety. The GANP 
encapsulates the framework that includes key civil aviation policies and principles 
where Regional and State Air Navigation Plans are required to be aligned to and 
also provides Regions and States with a comprehensive planning tool supporting 
the harmonization of global air navigation system.  
 
The GANP identifies all potential performance improvements available today, 
details the next generation of ground and avionics technologies that will be 
deployed worldwide, and provides the investment certainty needed for States to 
make strategic decisions for their individual planning purposes. 
 
The GANP includes the Aviation System Block Upgrade (ASBU) framework, its

deployed worldwide, and provides the investment certainty needed for States to 
make strategic decisions for their individual planning purposes. 
 
The GANP includes the Aviation System Block Upgrade (ASBU) framework, its 
modules and its associated technology roadmaps covering areas of; 
communications, surveillance, navigation, information management and avionics 
that will eventually realise a fully-harmonised global interoperable air navigation 
system, described within six-year timeframes for each ASBU Block starting with 
Block 0 in 2013 and continuing through 2031 and beyond (Refer Figure 1.1). 
ASBUs and the associated technology roadmaps are integral parts of the GANP 
and a valuable implementation tool kit.  
 
Deriving from the GANP, the Asia/Pacific- Regional Air Navigation Plan (RANP-
APAC) presents the framework for the APAC States in harmonising the APAC 
region with the global interoperable navigation system. Malaysia’s NANP is 
designed to be in harmony with the RANP-APAC and the ASBU framework 
included in the GANP.

improvement.

Although GANP is global in scope, it is not expected that all ASBU modules will 
be applied worldwide. Some of the ASBU modules contained in the GANP are 
specialised packages that must be applied wherever there are specific operational 
requirements or corresponding benefits. Table 1.2 contains comprehensive details 
about the ASBU elements. It is imperative to refer to this table to gain a 
comprehensive understanding of the ASBU elements. 
 
Considering the flexibility that ICAO has intentionally built into its Block Upgrade 
approach, there are nevertheless some elements of the GANP that will need to be 
considered for worldwide applicability. The characterisation of the particular Block 
Modules that are considered necessary for the future safety or regularity of 
international Air Navigation and which may eventually become an ICAO Standard, 
is essential to the success of the GANP.  
 
Compliance with existing standards is also key to this success. In this context, a 
wide synchronization of global or regional deployment timelines will sometimes be 
necessary as well as consideration with respect to possible implementation 
agreements or mandates.

Regional Air Navigation Plan (RANP) 
 
Regional Air Navigation Plan (RANP) represents the bridge between the global 
provisions in the ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs), the 
GANP and the States’ national plans and current implementation, and are 
developed to meet those needs of specific areas not covered in the worldwide 
provisions. 
 
RANP-APAC contains requirements related to the facilities and services to be 
implemented by the States in the APAC Region in accordance and is used as a 
repository document for the assignment of responsibilities to those States for the 
provision of required facilities and services within a specified area in accordance 
with Article 28 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation.

National Transportation Policy (NTP) 2019 – 2030 for Malaysia 
 
The Ministry of Transport’s National Transportation Policy 2019 – 2030, which has 
been completed and launched on 17 October 2019, covers a range of policies to 
increase 
and 
enhance 
the 
transportation 
industry 
through 
economic 
competitiveness, inclusivity, and accessibility to the public, in addition to reducing 
negative impact of the environmental and land use. 
 
The policy announced that any mode of transportation, including aviation should 
be oriented to safety, efficiency, enhanced competitiveness and integration with 
other modes of transportation, in addition to the sustainable development of 
transportation facilities and infrastructure to cater the growth in air traffic and 
aviation support services. 
 
The policy also recognises the need for different levels of development and 
process of continuous improvement under Malaysia’s aviation sector (i.e. in both 
safety and security); to comply with international Standards and Recommended 
Practices (SARPS) that have been set by the International Civil Aviation 
Organisations (ICAO). Developing guidance, sharing best practices and working 
in collaboration with industry partners on efficient use of infrastructure are 
therefore, important to achieve the policy objectives.

National Air Navigation Plan (NANP) for Malaysia 
 
The National Air Navigation Plan (NANP) Malaysia embraces the principle outlined 
in the National Transportation Policy (NTU) 2019 – 2030 and it is envisioned to 
foster the development of air navigation facilities and infrastructure with the 
overarching aim of establishing a secure, efficient, and dependable air transport 
network in Malaysia. It also stands as a testament to our commitment to align with 
the principles and aspirations set forth in the Global Air Navigation Plan (GANP) 
by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).  
 
As a signatory to ICAO's mandate for a seamless, safe, and efficient global air 
navigation system, our national plan serves as a localised manifestation of these 
global objectives. It reflects our dedication to adopting and adapting international 
standards, ensuring that our airspace management resonates with the broader 
harmonization efforts advocated by ICAO.

Introduction 
 
Airports stand as integral pillars within Malaysia's national economic infrastructure, 
serving as catalysts for investment, tourism, trade, and commerce. Their role 
extends beyond mere transportation hubs, actively propelling socio-economic 
growth across diverse sectors. To optimise national productivity and elevate 
economic performance, a continual commitment to investment and the 
modernization of aviation infrastructure at airports is imperative.  
 
The Malaysia NANP outlines the strategic initiatives and solutions aimed at 
enhancing airport operations, optimizing air traffic flow, and ensuring efficient 
utilization of airspace capacity within the Malaysia. These measures not only 
unlock the full spectrum of benefits but also guarantee the sustained, safe, and 
efficient operation of these vital hubs.

the Civil Aviation Act 1969 and the Civil Aviation (Aerodrome Operations) 
Regulations 2016.

Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM), is responsible for ensuring the

Communication, Navigation & Surveillance (CNS) 
 
Introduction 
 
Malaysia's NANP aims to establish a comprehensive framework for the planning 
and implementation of communication, navigation and surveillance (CNS) facilities 
and services. This document outlines the specific objectives and strategies align 
with ICAO Global and Regional plan to ensure the effective provision of air 
navigation services in compliance with ICAO SARPs.  
 
It is designed to enhance the safety, efficiency, and reliability of air navigation 
services. This plan includes the implementation of various technologies and 
procedures, each with specific objectives, detailed actions, and contributions to 
the overall air navigation system, including areas of communication, navigation 
and surveillance. 
 
Dynamic and Requirements 
 
This section details the dynamic elements related to the assignment of 
responsibilities for CNS facilities and services. It further outlines the mandatory 
requirements based on regional air navigation agreements and how they align with 
Article 28 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation. 
 
All CNS facilities and services provided in Malaysia are subjected to Civil Aviation 
Regulation 2016 (CAR), Regulation 158 and 159, and its associate fees and 
charges stipulated in Civil Aviation Regulation (Fees and Charges) 2016 
(CAR(FC)) and other relevant authorities regulations.

aim to enhance communication capabilities, supporting more efficient and 
direct communication between pilots and controllers, and improving overall 
efficiency and reliability.

The planning and provision of CNS facilities and services play a crucial role in the 
aviation industry. They are fundamental to ensuring safe, efficient, and economic 
operations. Among the key benefits include; 
a) Economy  
1) The Air Navigation Plan for Malaysia is designed to significantly improve 
the economic efficiency of air navigation services.  
2) The implementation of advanced communication, surveillance, and 
navigation technologies, such as ACARS, ATN/OSI, VDL Mode 2 Basic, 
SATCOM Class C Data, HFDL, SBAS, GBAS, ABAS, MON, will enhance 
the overall efficiency and reliability of these services.  
3) This will result in reduced operational costs, improved service delivery, 
and increased capacity, all of which contribute to the economic viability 
of the aviation industry. 
b) Efficiency

management, 
initial 
integration 
of 
time-based

enhanced surface guidance, and conflict alerting, as well as basic ATC

Introduction 
 
Malaysia's NANP aims to establish a comprehensive framework for the planning 
and implementation of air traffic management (ATM) facilities and services. This 
document outlines the specific objectives and strategies align with ICAO Global 
and Regional plan to ensure the effective provision of air navigation services in 
compliance with ICAO SARPs.  
 
It is designed to enhance the safety, efficiency, and reliability of air traffic 
management for the purpose of air navigation services. This plan includes the 
implementation of various technologies and procedures, each with specific 
objectives, detailed actions, and contributions to the overall air navigation system, 
including areas of communication, navigation and surveillance.

The analysis underscores a notable decline in air traffic movement during the 
tumultuous year of 2020, attributable to the global impact of the Covid-19 
pandemic. This downturn registered approximately a 60% reduction in 
international airport traffic and a 49% decrease in domestic airport movement. 
However, the forecasted data offers a glimmer of optimism, suggesting a 
resurgence in air travel by 2025. Projections indicate a remarkable recovery, 
with international airport traffic expected to surge by 193% and domestic airport 
activity forecasted to rebound by 49%, relative to 2020 levels. 
 
These insights provide invaluable guidance for aviation authorities, enabling 
informed decision-making in air traffic management strategies. By leveraging 
these projections, authorities can effectively plan and adapt infrastructure and 
services to accommodate the anticipated resurgence in air travel demand, 
ensuring optimal operational efficiency and passenger satisfaction in the years 
ahead.
